en: *Shoulengyan Jing Yishu Shiyao Chao*, Scroll One, with Preface. Compiled by the Śramaṇa Huaiyuan of Changshui.
The Great Master of Changshui, in his commentary on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, stated:
"As for the *Yishu* (Expository Commentary), it is essentially composed of the essential tenets of our own school."

The *Xiaojing* has been in circulation for a long time, yet its commentary (*chao*) is missing. One day, my disciples bowed their heads before me and requested that I compose a commentary to assist the sub-commentary (*shu*).
I told them, "The writings and meanings produced by our late master are as brilliant as the sun and moon; what need is there for further records?
The two or three disciples replied, "While these may be clear to the Master, they remain obscure to us. Therefore, [we beg you to compose it]."
Having obtained [the text], I have compiled this *Shiyao* (Essential Explanations) in six fascicles; as it elucidates the essential meanings of the *Śāstra*, it is titled accordingly.
Preface written on the full moon of the tenth month of the *Xinchou* year of the Jia-yu era, the fourth reign of the Great Song.

Regarding the commentary on this sūtra according to Changshui’s *Yìshù* (Commentary on the Meaning), there are two sections: first, the title; second, the explanation of the text. Within the first section, there are two parts: first, the explanation of the sūtra’s title;
second, the description of the author’s name. Now, for the first part: *Shòulăngyán Yìshù Zhùjīng* (Annotated Commentary on the Meaning of the Śūraṅgama Sūtra).
This seven-character title has three levels of broad and specific designations regarding the subject and object: first, the four characters "Śūraṅgama Sūtra" refer to that which is to be explained.

Regarding the three characters "Fǎtí yìshū zhù" (Commentary on the Meaning of the Title of the Dharma): "Néngjiě shūmù" (That Which Can Explain the Title of the Commentary) refers to the commentary itself;

"Shǒulèngyán" (Śūraṅgama) is the specific designation for the title of the dharma that is explained; and "Jīng" (Sūtra) is the general designation for that which explains. If one takes the general from the specific, it is not any other sūtra.
Alternatively, some say that "Shǒulèngyán" is the dharma that is explained and the character "Jīng" is that which explains; this is likely because [the former] is taken as the primary subject.

This refers to the principle that the ornamental patterns (kīra) mutually contain one another. The meaning is that the *Dharmadhātu-samādhi-sūtra*, which is the "principle" (*li*) to be expounded, subsumes both the "practice" (*xing*) and the "sūtra" (*jing*);
and the "sūtra" (*jing*) characters, which are the "expounding medium," subsume the three characters of "Śūraṅgama. This is like the way patterns appear within the interwoven threads of a brocade.

Third, while "Śūraṅgama" is restricted solely to this specific section (the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra*), it carries the sense of "discrimination" (*jian*); whereas the commentary on the sūtra (*shuzhu jing*) extends to other commentaries and other sūtras.
Because it is that which is to be distinguished, the *Śūraṅgama* is designated as the specific title for this commentary on the sutra.
*Śūraṅgama* is a term from the language of Central India; in the Song language, it means "the ultimate solidity of all phenomena.
When one has not yet cultivated this samādhi, all phenomena appear distinct and one is bound by them; when one attains this samādhi, mountains, rivers, and the great earth...

The earth, color, emptiness, light, darkness, and all phenomena are quiescent in their very place; this is precisely the eternally abiding nature of mind. Therefore, it is said to be the "ultimately firm" [Dharma].
As the *Lotus Sūtra* says, "The characteristics of the world are eternally abiding. An ancient master said, "There is no dharma outside the mind; the blue mountains fill the eyes.
However, while the title of this present sūtra consists of twenty characters, only three are designated as its core. It is for this reason.
These three characters precisely indicate the wondrous practice of the Middle Way, manifesting the true essence of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

Since all sentient beings and all Buddhas share this same single source, Tiantai said: "The quiescence of the Dharma-realm is called *śamatha* (calm abiding); its constant illumination within that quiescence is called *vipaśyanā* (insight).

As these constitute the essential core of this sutra—the path cultivated by the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time—this commentary extracts the most concise and vital points to serve as its title.
Question: The three characters "Dàfóding" (Great Buddha-Crown) precisely expound the wondrous principle of the Three Virtues (*triguṇa*), which is what this entire sutra reveals.

Why is this not used as the title? Answer: From the perspective of verbal expression, when one is in a state of delusion, it pertains to phenomena (*dharma*). "Śūraṅgama" refers to practice; because taking the principle as the immediate goal, it is so designated.
However, as the Master said: "Although the essence is remote, the Perfect and Sudden is real; although the First Principle is the principle, when compared [to the title],..."
Observing that [the title] pertains to the subject matter, one knows that *Śūraṅgama* is the most essential;
however, if one were to follow the convenience of the characters, the single character "sūtra" (*jing*) would have been placed below the three characters "Śūraṅgama.

Because we here follow the convenience of the meaning, it is placed at the end, as this is a commentary (*yi-shu*) that explains the text of the sūtra. It is also to use the general term "sūtra" below to manifest its specific application above.

The above [section] specifically clarifies the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*, while the following section provides a general exposition (and so forth). △ Regarding the meaning (*artha*), the glossary states that it signifies "appropriateness" (*yī*);
this means that one regulates and arranges matters and things so that they become appropriate. The intent of the commentary (*shū*) is stated as follows:

"I shall now directly explain the scriptural text based on the meaning of the perfect and real (*yuan-shí*), rather than further elaborating on its interpretation by way of the various teachings of the five periods. △ Commentary (*shū*).

"Zhè" (者) refers to "zhāo" (條), meaning the systematic arrangement and the underlying significance of the scriptural text. Furthermore, the *Wénxīn diáolóng* states: "Sū" (疏) means "to spread out" (*bù*);

it refers to laying out the fundamental points of the subject matter and summarizing the proximate meanings of the titles. Regarding the character for "zhù" (註): it is sometimes written with the radical "water" (*shuǐ*) and sometimes with the radical "speech" (*yán*).
If it takes the radical "speech," it is because one provides commentary and explanation of the scriptural text through words. If it takes the radical "water," it is as follows: [text continues]
Water from a single source, if it does not flow forth, has no means of moistening things; if it does not flow forth, by what means can it benefit life?
Therefore, it now flows forth to benefit the multitude of sentient beings. Furthermore, "commentary" (*zhù*) carries the meaning of being linked and attached together;

it refers to using principles (*yì*) to annotate beneath the scriptures (*jīng*), so that there are principles beneath the scriptures and categories (*kē*) preserved above the principles, thereby preventing them from being left to run wild.
It is easy for people to understand that this is distinguished from other commentaries by being circulated separately from the sūtra. △ "Sūtra" (jing) is explained as "dharma" and "permanence.
Dharma is that which serves as the track for all capacities; permanence is that which is proclaimed by all the sages. Therefore, it is called a "sūtra. Furthermore, "sūtra" means "path.
This sūtra is the universal path by which the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time proceed toward reality. △ "Scroll" (juan) refers to that which can be rolled up and unrolled. △
"Di" (第) means "to dwell. △ First, the opening of the numerical sequence.
Second, the description of the author's name. △ "Changshui" (長水) is the name of a river in Xiuzhou. △ "Śramaṇa" (沙門), when fully expressed, is *śramaṇa*;
this is translated as "one who exhausts the path. Because he serves as a fertile field of merit, he is able to sever the famine of sentient beings through cultivation.
Because of the Eightfold Noble Path, one is able to sever all wrong paths; thus, the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* says:
"To sever all lack and to sever all wrong paths—therefore, one who cultivates the Eightfold Noble Path is called a śramaṇa. It is also translated as "diligent rest" (and so forth).

Although there should be the character for "explanation" (*śāsana*), it is not included here because there are no non-Buddhist paths (tīrthikas) in this land. As for the non-Buddhists of the Western regions...

Because he is called a śramaṇa, the term "Śākya" is added to distinguish him; likewise, because there are those of the Śākya clan who do not leave the household life, the term "śramaṇa" is added to distinguish him.
Since there are these two potential confusions, he is referred to as "Śramaṇa-Śākya. As for "Zixuan," this is the high honorific name (gaomíng) of the author of the commentary.
His original name was Zixuan, his courtesy name was Zhongwei, and his native village was in Qiantang. His secular surname was Zheng.
He shaved his head under a master at Pumen Temple on Mount Nan-shan; because he studied under the Dharma Master Hongmin, the Monk-Judge of Jiaxing, he adopted the moniker Changshui.

During the Tianxi era, Huien, the Abbot of the Tiantai School and Grand Master Chongjiao, petitioned for him to enter the mountains to lecture on this sutra, whereupon he was granted an imperial purple robe by decree. During the Tiānshèng era, [he resided] in Qiantang.
The Provincial Governor, Vice Minister Hu, requested that a lecture be held at Xiangfu Temple; the assembly of clergy and laity numbered nearly one thousand.
An imperial posthumous title was bestowed upon him, naming him the Great Master Lengyan.

Furthermore, the author of the preface, whose nature was divinely gifted for the wondrous realization of this sutra, had previously, due to the earnest requests of Chan masters from various quarters, composed a single manual for the ritual of expounding the sutra, which is currently in circulation.

When the world had generally lectured on this sutra up to thirty times, he encountered the earnest invitation of Master Gyeongnam of Haegwan Baesoyon, who requested him to compose a sub-commentary (*shu*).
Consequently, he went to that monastery and held his pen for ninety days until the single commentary was completed.

Among the eminent monks throughout the land and the distinguished scholars of the court, there were none who did not revere it or delight in its study. △ "Ji" (集) means to gather; [as defined by] Liu Xi.

Just as one gathers various colored threads to form brocade and embroidery, or gathers various characters to form words and meanings, so too has the Master of the Commentary gathered various meanings to compose this commentary; this is also an expression of humility.
The second section, the verses of homage and petition, has two parts. First, the homage to the Triple Gem: this single verse is entirely the words of Master Zizhong Huang;
the commentator [of the present work] preserved it because his own school follows Zizhong’s commentary and he did not wish to forget its original intent.

Now, regarding the taking refuge in the Triple Gem, there are variations in what is included or omitted: some take refuge in the Buddha alone, some take refuge in the person [the Buddha] alone, and some...
Generally, those who do not offer a dedication each follow their own intentions; however, this commentary includes a full dedication.

It is for six reasons that one takes refuge in the Three Jewels: first, the debt of gratitude, meaning that the Buddha’s great compassion bestowed the teachings and the Sangha led me from suffering to the attainment of happiness; thus, the Three Jewels have rendered me a great service.

First, one takes refuge out of gratitude for the Buddha’s benevolence; second, one takes refuge to request his protection, meaning that as one intends to compose this commentary, there is fear of many demonic disturbances and obstacles arising;

third, one takes refuge to inspire faith, meaning that since the Master’s wisdom was not yet perfected, there might be little faith in the commentary he composed, but now, by relying on the Buddha’s power, it will certainly be believed.

There is no doubt that because there are ritual protocols for the fourfold composition, the way of a minister or a son requires that one must first inform their sovereign or father before undertaking any action.
Now, this descendant of the Dharma, about to engage in compilation, must first take refuge in the Triple Gem as his ultimate model.

Thus, he honors the five [aspects] to manifest their supreme excellence; for the Triple Gem is most venerable, standing preeminent above all things, and serves as the fertile field for the world. This opening homage expresses such intent.

Because they are supreme, six [aspects] are for the benefit of sentient beings; because the Three Jewels have the capacity to extensively benefit all classes of beings, yet the ignorant and foolish do not perceive this and few know it, one specifically takes refuge in them to manifest that there is great benefit for all things.
△ "Prostrating" (kai-shou) refers to the sincere resolve of the one who takes refuge. "Kai" (pronounced *ji*) means to touch the head to the ground and remain there for a short time.
This is the most solemn among the nine types of prostrations (*navavidha-praṇāma*). As for the nine prostrations: first is the *kai-shou* (the prostration with the head touching the ground);
second is the *ton-shou*, which means striking the head against the ground; third is the *kong-shou*, where the head reaches the hands, which is the standard bowing of the head;

fourth is the *chen-dong*, which involves changing one's facial expression as if in mourning or repentance; fifth is the *ji-bai*, which refers to performing the prostration first and then the *ke-sang* (touching the forehead to the ground). It is said that...

Sixth, those wearing the *qícuī* (mourning dress of hemp) for periods from one year downward perform the "Mourning Bow" (*xiōngbài*): first bowing the head to the ground (*jǐmǎng*) and then performing the prostration.
Seventh, those wearing the three-year mourning dress perform the "Odd Bow" (*qíbài*, pronounced as *jī*): first bending one knee. Eighth, the "Exalted Bow" (*bāobài*):

that is, the double prostration. Ninth, the "Reverential Bow" (*sùbài*): merely bowing the body and lowering the hands; those in armor and helmets do not prostrate, but simply perform a salutation (*yī*). Now it says:
"Prostrating oneself" (*kai-shou*) refers to a most reverent salutation. One who is able to take refuge must necessarily possess the three types of action (*trikarma*).

Taking refuge through the action of the body (*kāyakarma*) manifests that the Buddha possesses the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) to see; taking refuge through the action of speech (*vākkarma*) manifests that the Buddha possesses the divine ear (*divyaśrotra*) to hear;

and taking refuge through the action of mind (*manaskarma*) manifests that the Buddha possesses the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) to know. Prior to this taking of refuge, all three types of action were entirely unwholesome; through taking refuge, they are transformed.
The latter three karmas are all wholesome. Furthermore, by dedicating the bodily karma from the causal stage to the fruition, one obtains the wheel of supernatural powers;
by dedicating the verbal karma to the fruition, one obtains the wheel of correct teaching; and by dedicating the mental karma to the fruition, one obtains the wheel of knowing others' minds.
Because these wheels can crush and grind away karma and afflictions, I prostrate to the Dharma and Sangha who turn these wheels. △ My Great Master, below...
The six phrases refer to the Three Jewels to which one takes refuge; these are of three types: the institutional (zhuchi), the distinct characteristics (biexiang), and the identical essence (tongti).

Regarding the institutional: cast, engraved, modeled, or painted [images] are called the Buddha; the teachings of the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Śāstras are called the Dharma; and those with shaven heads and dyed robes are called the Saṃgha. Regarding the distinct characteristics:

the Buddha refers to the three bodies (trikāya) or the ten bodies; the Dharma refers to the teaching, principle, practice, and fruit; and the Saṃgha refers to the three stages of worthiness (sankuan) and the ten stages of sagehood (shisheng).

Nevertheless, there are differences in the depth of the five teachings because the three bodies (trikāya) and so forth are each distinct; thus, they are called "distinct characteristics" (pṛthaglakṣaṇa).

As for "identical essence" (samāna-svabhāva), it refers to the fact that within a single dharma, there is the meaning of awakened illumination, which is called the Buddha; it can be taken as a standard and maintained, which is called the Dharma;
and the harmony of wisdom and various virtues is called the Saṃgha. Now, among these three, this sutra follows the revelation of the provisional after [the establishment of the real].

This explanation states that [the term] "I" (ātman) refers primarily to the One Body while secondarily extending to the other two bodies; the character for "I" applies to both the subject who takes refuge and the object to which one takes refuge.
If it belongs to the subject who takes refuge, it means "I bow my head before my Great Teacher"; if it belongs to the object to which one takes refuge, it is to designate the Buddha as "I.

Yet, since the Buddha-dharma is without self (*anātman*), why is he called "I"? It is said that this is to distinguish between "self" and "other"; thus, among the four kinds of "self," this is the "self" as it is conventionally circulated in the world.
That which is penetrated consists of both the conventional and the ultimate. △ The "Great Master" (Mahāśramaṇa) is one among the ten titles [of a Buddha];

however, this single phrase applies exclusively to Śākyamuni Buddha alone, as he is the presiding teacher for this world-system. △ The "Venerable Tamer of the Ten Directions" (Daśadig-vināyaka-guru) applies universally to all, signifying that all Buddhas have realized the same truth;
that is to say, their single mind, single wisdom, powers, and fearlessnesses are likewise identical. Furthermore—
This distinguishes [the Buddha] from those of the Two Vehicles who do not believe in Buddhas of other directions, acknowledging only Śākyamuni as the one [Buddha].
△ Regarding the "Tamer" (Vināyaka), the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "The Tathāgata possesses four wholesome dharmas for taming sentient beings.

△ Because he is honored by devas and humans, and because he possesses the aforementioned nine titles, he receives the appellation "Venerable" (Bhagavat). △ The final two phrases below "Buddha" (Buddha) praise the Dharma Jewel.

There are four kinds: namely, the Dharma of Teaching, the Dharma of Practice, the Dharma of Fruit, and the Dharma of Distinction. First, the Buddha-Crown (Buddhoṣṇīṣa) refers to the Dharma of Teaching; as stated below:
"Although one has received the Buddha-Crown Divine Mantra of the Tathāgata. Second, Śūraṅgama refers to the Dharma of Practice; as stated below:

"There is a Great Buddha-Crown named Śūraṅgama, which is fully endowed with the ten thousand practices. Third, Great Enlightenment refers to the Dharma of Fruit; that is, ultimate enlightenment (*atyanta-bodhi*). It serves to distinguish this from similar states.
Because it is true, it is called the Great Enlightenment (Mahābodhi). △ The Tathāgatagarbha is the principle-dharma (*dharmatā*) and also the fruit of the *Uṣṇīṣa*;

it is the practice of the *Śūraṅgama*. The Tathāgatagarbha of Great Enlightenment is the principle-dharma; as stated below, because these three are explained within the arising of emptiness, they are called the "Teaching-Dharma Treasury" (*śāsana-dharmakośa*).
"Treasury" (*kośa*) has the meaning of containing and storing; its essence possesses all virtues. △ Below, "Perfectly Bright" (*paripūrṇa-avabhāsa*)...
The two lines praising the Sangha Jewel’s perfect clarity refer to the twenty-five sages who have all realized perfect clarity;
alternatively, they may praise only Avalokiteśvara (and so forth). △ "All the Sages" refers to the entire assembly of listeners;
alternatively, it may mean that all sages are Great Beings of Perfect Clarity. △ "The Dragon King Nāgarāja as the Foremost" specifically praises Mañjuśrī.

In a previous kalpa prior to the Bodhisattva’s attainment of the Way, he was named Nāgarāja-rāja (Dragon Honored King); now, in his present traces, he abides in the causal stage, assisting the Capable Sage (Śākyamuni).
His wisdom and virtue transcend the multitudes, serving as the leader for the assembly; therefore, he is called "The Foremost" (*agrasatva*) above, and "Mañjuśrī acting as the Foremost" below.

△ "Constantly opening," etc., is a general praise of his great compassion. "Opening" means to open wide; it refers to constantly opening the gate of great compassion to deliver and liberate [sentient beings].

The term "gate" (*môn*) has the meaning of being able to penetrate without obstruction; however, there are distinctions between the gate of teaching (*chiao-môn*), the gate of practice (*haeng-môn*), and the gate of principle (*ri-môn*).
Compassion (*ji*) is able to bestow happiness, while pity (*bi*) is able to extract suffering.

Since it is said that compassion bestows happiness and pity extracts suffering, it follows that what is capable of saving is precisely pity—meaning that the Buddha saves and extracts suffering from sentient beings by means of the four methods of attraction (*catvāri saṃgrahavastūni*). △ This refers to... [text truncated]

The Three Jewels are those who rescue and gather in sentient beings. △ [This is] the vow to descend and fulfill the aspiration to benefit living beings; "vow" (*praṇidhāna*) here carries the sense of longing and desire.
The Master of the Commentary, being about to compose this commentary, fears that many demonic disturbances may arise, and thus begs for the bestowal of majestic power.
Furthermore, this wondrous and inconceivable Dharma is profound and hidden; its teaching, principle, practice, and fruit are all beyond thought. Were it not for the Three Jewels...
If one does not augment and increase wisdom, there will be no means to understand and penetrate the profound meaning; thus, the *Lotus Sūtra* says:

"Even if the entire world were filled with those like Śāriputra, and they were to exhaust their thoughts to measure it together, they could not fathom the Buddha’s wisdom. Since even the sagely wisdom is difficult to conceive or calculate, how much more so for ordinary people?

Therefore, one must pray for the bestowal of protection. There are two kinds of such protection: the hidden (*míng*) and the manifest (*xiǎn*). The hidden refers simply to seeking [protection] in a latent manner.
One should secretly assist his power of wisdom so that he may manifest his body, place his hand upon one's head, preach the Dharma, and offer consolation;
for now, we merely pray for his hidden grace. However, a detailed discussion of the hidden and the manifest includes four propositions, thirty-six propositions, and so forth.
△ "I" refers to the Master himself, the author of the commentary. △ "Manifest preaching" refers to the Master’s wisdom. △ "Subtle and inconceivable" refers to this very teaching, namely:

I wish to clarify and proclaim this wondrous and inconceivable teaching through this commentary; since both the means of expression and that which is expressed are beyond conceptual thought, it is termed "wondrous.

Furthermore, as we enter the final age of strife and contention, fearing that those with divergent attachments will largely disparage it, I pray that the Triple Gem will provide protection so that no harm shall come to it. △ Below, "universally together," etc., is the dedication for all sentient beings.
The intent of this commentary on the sutra is solely for the benefit of sentient beings. "All sentient beings" (*hanling*) is a variant term for "living beings" (*zhongsheng*).

Furthermore, because the Dharma-character school (*xiangzong*) asserts that those who hold to "three non-existences and two existences" cannot attain Buddhahood, [the author] specifically concludes by addressing "all sentient beings.
"Swiftly realizing the ocean of True Suchness" means that it does not intend to cause beings to realize the fruits of the realms of humans, devas, or *śrāvakas*.

This is because one desires to cause all sentient beings to equally realize the ultimate ocean of fruition that is True Suchness (*tathatā*). The phrase "ocean of True Suchness" employs both a dharma-term and a metaphor together.
"True" (*zhen*) means being free from all falsehood and delusion; "Suchness" (*ru*) means having neither going nor coming.

The Dharma-nature is all-pervasive and, like the ocean, is vast and great. Because it is free from falsehood and delusion, it is like the ocean’s clarity and purity; there is no dharma not contained within it, just as with the ocean.
Precious treasures are compared to the ocean for this reason.
Regarding the explanation of the text below, there are two parts; first, the division of the chapters. △ "Jiang" (將) means "intending to" or "provisionally.

△ First, concerning the causes and conditions for the arising of the teaching: Now, when a sage establishes a teaching, it is certainly not in vain. What is the purpose for which this sutra has arisen?
For this reason, he was granted the teaching to initiate its causal conditions; through these ten causes and conditions, the teaching was brought forth.

Once the teaching had arisen, it was not yet known whether, in terms of the Dharma or the person, it was subsumed under which Piṭaka. Therefore, the next section distinguishes the inclusion within the Piṭakas and Vehicles.

The Piṭakas encompass both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, and among Bodhisattvas there are those of provisional and ultimate capacities; if one does not seek them according to their underlying meaning, one will fail to understand their essential intent.

Since it is already known that this sūtra is subsumed within the Bodhisattva-piṭaka and collected in the Sūtra-piṭaka, one may wonder: what is the ultimate limit of the scope of the Dharma it elucidates?

Thus, there is the third [section], the "Limit of the Meaning of the Teaching," which clarifies that the meaning taught by the teaching has reached its ultimate extent. However, as for which specific types of practitioners are capable of awakening and entering into it, this is not yet fully understood;
therefore, there is the fourth [section], the "Appropriate Capacity of Those to be Taught," which concerns those who are to be taught by the meaning thus elucidated.

Since this has already been clarified, it is not yet known what constitutes the essence of the teaching that expresses [the meaning]. Therefore, there is the fifth [section] on the essence of the expressive teaching (*vācaka-śarīra*).
Once the essence of the teaching is elucidated, one must consider the subject matter (*abhidheya*) expressed by that teaching and toward what its ultimate purpose (*prayojana*) tends.
Therefore, there is the sixth [section] on the subject matter and its ultimate purpose. Having understood that this sūtra is based upon the *tathāgatagarbha*, [the following is established].
Taking the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* as the primary theme, because it is not yet clear at what time this sutra was preached, the seventh section clarifies the chronological sequence of the teachings;

although it is known that it was preached after the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and before the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*, it is still not clear in what year it was transmitted to the Eastern Land (China), when it was translated, or by whom.
Therefore, the eighth section clarifies the year of the transmission and translation; since this is already known...
Regarding the title at the beginning of this scripture established during the era of its translation:
since one must necessarily have prior knowledge of the overall framework that serves as the summary for this entire work, the ninth section provides a general explanation of the title.

As for the statement in the outline, "General Explanation of the Title," this means explaining the title in a comprehensive manner (and so forth). Although the main outlines are distinguished, the internal meanings branch out in a thousand directions like doors and windows. If...
Because the meaning of "extensive explanation" (*vyākhyā*) is difficult to understand, there is a tenth section consisting of a detailed explanation of the text and its meaning.

△ Regarding the "detailed explanation of the text and its meaning," this refers to the interpretation of the specific words and meanings [of the scripture] (and so forth). Now, among these ten sections, the first eight constitute a preliminary discourse, while the final two explain the sūtra.

This tenfold structure was established by Fazhen (Fahsien); if one correlates it with the Tiantai system of the fivefold profound meaning (*pañca-vidha-gambhīrārtha*), it corresponds to the category of "person" (*pudgala*).

The essence of the Tathāgatagarbha-mind is the *śūraṅgama-samādhi*; its primary purpose is to shatter doubts and give rise to faith, taking the "clarified butter" (*tīrāmṛta*) as its doctrinal characteristic (and so forth).

Second, the sequential commentary on the ten sections: first, the division of the text within the "Causes and Conditions. △ Regarding the general and specific: the general refers to the entirety of the one lifetime [of the Buddha], while the specific refers to each individual part.

In this sutra, there are two parts to the correct explanation. First, within the general section, the causes and conditions are correctly demonstrated. △ "To repay" (chou) means to recompense. △ "Cause" refers to the stage of the Buddha;
at the time of the causal stage, desiring to analyze and attain unsurpassed bodhi, he thus initiated the Four Great Vows: the vow to [extinguish] afflictions...
He vowed to sever the dharmas, to learn the path, to deliver sentient beings, and to perfect the Buddha-way; yet these four vows are merely the two gates of compassion and wisdom.
Wisdom is already perfected, but compassion remains incomplete. Regarding the vow to deliver sentient beings, it remains vividly present;

thus, although he has now realized the fruit, he does not abandon the gate of causes, manifesting his body and preaching the teachings to rescue and deliver all living beings in order to fulfill his original vows.
Therefore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "In the past, I established this vow: 'I desire to cause all sentient beings to be no different from myself.
Now that my former vows have been fulfilled, I transform all sentient beings and cause them universally to enter the Buddha-way."
△ Regarding the "Request": This refers to the Buddhas’ initial attainment of the Way, when Brahmā, Śakra, and the various devas requested him to turn the Wheel of Dharma. As the Sūtra says:

Because he came and silently accepted the invitation, beginning at the Deer Park and ending at the Śāla grove, he preached various sūtras and dharmas to teach and transform sentient beings.
As the Sūtra says, "At Vārāṇasī, he turned the wheel of the Four Noble Truths," and so forth; thus it is called "repaying the invitation."

△ Regarding those who manifest the principles to deliver sentient beings: teaching the Dharma to manifest the principles is truly for the purpose of delivering sentient beings. Now, the term "manifesting the principles" encompasses both the general and the specific.
If one speaks the Dharma with a single voice such that each type of being understands it according to their own kind, this is the general [teaching].

If one speaks of the Four Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination to manifest the principle of the emptiness of sentient beings and deliver ordinary people and non-Buddhists, or speaks of the Dharma of the Six Pāramitās to manifest the [emptiness of] phenomena... [the second level].
By means of the principle of emptiness, those of the two vehicles whose nature is not yet fixed and those sentient beings of sharp faculties are led to enter the Mahāyāna path;
by expounding the ultimate Dharma of the One Vehicle, the principle of the true mark is revealed.

This leads those of fixed nature, those of unfixed nature, those who are perfect Bodhisattvas, and ordinary persons of the highest faculties to enter the ultimate Buddha-way. However, if this single period is analyzed in detail, it can be further divided into four [stages].

The Four Truths, the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, and the Six Pāramitās each have distinct versions in the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, as well as provisional and ultimate forms; their manifestations of principle also differ.
For example, regarding the Four Truths, there are the truths of birth-and-death, non-arising, the immeasurable, and the unconditioned (and so forth).

Tiantai explains that the *Zàng* and *Tōng* teachings manifest the principle of true emptiness (*zhēn kōng lǐ*), while the *Bié* and *Yuán* teachings manifest the principle of the Middle Way (*zhōng dào lǐ*). In the latter, true existence is both identical to and not identical with [emptiness].

Within this, it is not merely that, according to the present sutra, after the provisional teachings have been opened, the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna are universally gathered so that all may realize the *tathāgatagarbha* (the hidden heart);
rather, it is the single, ultimate reality. **II. To precisely discuss the Buddha’s intention.** **A. To thoroughly investigate:** "To thoroughly" (*yuan*) means to exhaustively probe.

The Master of the *Tianchang* Commentary explains: "The Buddha’s knowledge and vision is neither three nor five; therefore, it is called 'one'."
Because it is vast and all-encompassing, it is called "Great. Because this birth by transformation is taught as the ritual practice of all Buddhas, it is called "the matter" (*shi*).

The stimulus that moves [the Buddha] is called the "cause" (*in*), and the Buddha’s response is the "condition" (*en*); this is the reason why [he appears]. It is for the sake of these great causes and conditions that he manifests in the world.

Tiantai explains this through the contemplation of the mind via four stages, four wisdoms, and four gates. Regarding the four stages, "opening" refers to the beginning of the Ten Abidings.

Only when one internally augments the power of contemplation and externally relies upon the rain of Dharma to eliminate both the general and specific delusions will the knowledge and vision of inherent virtue shine forth clearly, and [the Tathāgatagarbha] be opened.

"Arising" (*fa*) indicates the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*); since the delusive obstructions have been removed, the essence of knowledge and vision is revealed, and the myriad virtues of the *dharmadhātu* are displayed with clarity.

"Awakening" (*wu*) refers to the ten stages of dedication (*daśa-pratipatti*); because the obstructions are removed and the essence is revealed, the principle of the *dharmadhātu* becomes clear—hence it is called "awakening.
"Entering" (*ru*) refers to the ten grounds (*daśa-bhūmi*); as phenomena and principle are now harmonized, one attains sovereign non-obstruction from the letter *A* to the letter *Ḍa*.
However, in the case of the "flowing-in" (nyūryū), because one stage is all stages, it is explained as being non-different yet different. Regarding other meanings, they are detailed elsewhere;

here, I shall state the essential point: that which can know and see is the wondrous wisdom of the Perfect and Sudden (en-don), and that which is known and seen is the wondrous principle of the True Aspect (jissō).

"If one attains the wondrous arousal of true *samādhi*, then the wondrous is eternally quiescent; both existence and non-existence are absent, and even this 'absence of duality' is extinguished.

This immediately serves to clarify the permanence of the nature by means of the analogy of looking at a river. △ Regarding the "Investigation of the Mind in Seven Locations":

Why, then, does the Tathāgata suddenly abandon cause and condition by saying, 'I attained awakening through the mind based on cause and condition,' and so forth? This [objection] has already been refuted previously regarding the cause.
Because he now harbors doubts once again, it is called "a second reprimand.
4. Severing the Net of Doubt. △ *Jue* (決) means to resolve or clarify completely. △ *Duan* (斷) means to sever or eliminate. When various matters are not one, it is called "the multitude" (*zhong*).
To be hesitant and unclear regarding the principle is called "doubt" (*yi*). Doubt covers the true reality like a net that traps and obscures. △ *Shi* (示) means to demonstrate.
When the Seer realized that his faculty of vision was originally and eternally present through the Buddha’s manifestation, he asked:

"Although I recognize this nature of vision as being non-reversible, how do I know it is my true nature? The Buddha employed his supernormal powers to cause him to see into the first dhyāna, intending to reveal that the true vision is all-pervasive and originally such.
Since merit and fault reside in the person, the vision manifests as either distant or near; therefore, the Buddha [proceeded] accordingly.
Bodhisattvas who have exhausted the Dharma-realm can see hundreds of thousands of worlds and even sentient beings, yet their vision does not exceed a mere inch when looking through a hole.
Regarding "contraction and severance": when Ānanda returned to the lecture hall, he saw only what was within a single room.
Having just seen the distant, he now saw only the narrow; consequently, he doubted whether this was a contraction of the large into the small, or whether it was simply a wall.

Because the command to "fold the space" was given, it is called "contracting and cutting. The Buddha then used the metaphor of emptying a vessel to illustrate this, so that [the disciples] would know that emptiness has no fixed dimensions;
whether the vessel is square or round, when viewed together, there is neither expansion nor contraction. △ Regarding "detaching from the body":
as the Buddha showed, all sentient beings since beginningless time have been deluded, taking themselves to be objects. If one can turn these objects around, then...
The Tathāgata’s body and mind are perfectly luminous and immovable within the site of enlightenment, capable of universally containing the lands of the ten directions.

Ānanda, however, did not understand that his own true vision was all-pervasive and transcended the distinction between self and other; instead, he sought to turn back the external objects before him to constitute his own true vision.
Therefore, he doubted, saying: "If this essence of vision were truly my wondrous nature, it would now be present before me."
"My present body and mind—what are they? and so forth; this refers to Ānanda’s thought that the nature of seeing exists upon external objects.
The Tathāgata consequently refuted this extensively by means of the "seeing" and "non-seeing" of those objective phenomena. Regarding the phrase "conditions are naturally so":

because Ānanda sought to discern whether seeing or non-seeing existed upon objective phenomena and found neither to be obtainable, the Tathāgata confirmed all of this, saying: [the conditions are naturally so].
Thus it was; because this great assembly was thus bewildered and lost its bearings, Mañjuśrī inquired of them:
"What is the fundamental nature of seeing? Because there is no characteristic of right or wrong, the Tathāgata showed them:

"The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, within the samādhi of their own intrinsic nature, perceive both the act of seeing and the objects of seeing as being like flowers in the sky; they are fundamentally bodhi."

How can this wondrous, pure, and luminous essence contain within it "is" and "is not"? Furthermore, because one suspects that the nature of seeing is a phenomenon produced by causes and conditions or is something spontaneous, the text below asks:

"Truly, as the Dharma King has said, what difference is there between this 'awakened awareness pervading the ten directions' and the 'divine self (ātman) pervading the ten directions' discussed by the non-Buddhists? Since it is certainly not spontaneous, [it must be...]
Regarding these causes and conditions, what is the meaning of their conformity with the nature of causes and conditions?
△ As for "conjunction yet not conjoined," it was because the Buddha pointed out that when one sees seeing, that seeing is not [true] seeing; failing to understand this principle, he then asked:

"Conjunction yet not conjoined—the mind has not yet clarified this, and now hearing further that 'seeing seeing is not seeing,' my confusion and distress increase all the more. Therefore, the Buddha...
Each [objection] shall be refuted in turn. △ Regarding the doubt concerning the nature [of reality] due to clinging to characteristics:

This refers to Pūrṇa, who, upon hearing the Tathāgata say that "the nature of fire is true emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is true fire; it is pure and fundamental, pervading the Dharma-realm," and so forth, became suspicious because he clung to the distinct characteristics of conditioned arising.
He thus doubted that within the nature, these characteristics could not be harmoniously integrated. Therefore, the text says: "World-Honored One, if earth..."
"How can the nature of water pervade everywhere and yet allow for the presence of water, while the nature of fire does not arise?
Furthermore, how do you explain that the natures of water and fire both pervade the Dharma-realm without one subduing or extinguishing the other? The Buddha then refuted this, saying:

"To contemplate their characteristics as fundamentally false is to have nothing that can be pointed out or described; it is like seeking to tie empty flowers together to form empty fruit. To contemplate their nature as fundamentally true is simply wondrous, enlightened clarity."
Since the awakened, luminous mind was originally neither water nor fire, why do you again ask about the principle of their mutual overcoming and extinction?
Regarding the "extinguishing delusion to give rise to further delusion," Pūrṇa’s doubt is as follows: "All sentient beings and the Buddha’s nature of awakening are fundamentally pure;

yet, without apparent cause, mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arose. Now that the Tathāgata has attained the wondrous, empty, luminous awakening, when will such things arise once more?"

One might mistakenly think: "Since sentient beings are fundamentally pure, they have suddenly given rise to delusion; now that the Tathāgata has extinguished this delusion, when will they ever give rise to delusion again?
To refute this, the Tathāgata employs four analogies—mistaking directions, flowers in the sky, gold ore, and ash-wood.
Regarding the phrase "becoming true or not true," it is stated below: "All dharmas are entirely the true essence of attaining Buddhahood."
An objection may be raised: "The Buddha has already attained the Way; how can there now still be the distinctions of the seven realms of existence, such as the hells?
This would imply that after the false phenomena have been merged with the Truth, something untrue exists once again. Alternatively, these two phrases may be intended to convey a single meaning.

Regarding the phrase "cultivating the causes of impermanence," etc., the subsequent sutra states that the Buddha requires the practitioner to generate the mind of the ground (the causal stage) so that it corresponds with the mind of the fruit (the resultant stage).
If they do not correspond, supreme enlightenment will ultimately never be accomplished—just as one who sows bitter seeds seeking sweetness, or steams sand to make rice.
Ānanda, as the Buddha has said: "The awakened mind of the causal stage must correspond with the designations of the resultant stage.
If, within the resultant stage, there are bodhi, nirvāṇa, true thusness (tathatā), buddha-nature, the amala-vijñāna, emptiness, and the Tathāgata...
The Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom within the *garbha* is the essence of seven names, its nature firm and solid like a diamond king.

If this seeing and hearing are free from light and darkness and ultimately lack substantiality, how can one take this ultimate cessation as a cause for cultivation, desiring to obtain the Tathāgata’s fruit of the seven eternal abidings?
The Tathāgata caused Rāhu to strike a bell to manifest the nature of the mind.
The phrase "non-extinguishing function" (*amṛta-vṛtti*) is used to resolve those doubts.

Fifth, the exposition on cultivation (*pratipatti*). "Discrimination" (*vibhāga*) means analytical discernment; it ensures that the provisional and the ultimate do not become confused, and that the heterodox and the orthodox are clearly distinguished.

△ "The Gate" refers to practice (*pratipatti*), for it is that which enables one to reach the principle of the fruit. △ "Profound Understanding Manifesting" means that the essence of the *pitaka* is difficult to know;
yet, through the Buddha’s skillful means, it has already been made clear and certain. If one does not practice, what benefit is there in the understanding of emptiness?

Even if one has heard much, it is equal to not having heard at all. Therefore, following this, he requests the method of practice, so as to subsequently create the path leading to reality. Thus, below...
Please say: "Suddenly I have been granted a magnificent mansion by the Heavenly King; though I have obtained this great residence, I must enter through the gate.

The Heavenly King is a metaphor for the Buddha, and the house is a metaphor for the *tathāgatagarbha*. If one wishes to enter the nature of the *garbha* and abide therein, one must necessarily enter through the gates of practice;
therefore, the Buddha has taught the two gates of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* as the essentials of cultivation, through which the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time have realized Bodhi.
"Also. △ "Reaching" means to arrive at. △ "Chou" (疇) is a particle; because of the delusion of beginningless time, it is called "clinging to conditions from the past" (*pān-yüan*).
△ "Determined" (*ching-ting*) means that the Buddhas of the three periods of time must certainly rely upon this. △ "Tranquil" (*chan*) is synonymous with "stopping" (*chi*).

△ "Immediately subduing" means using meditative concentration (*samādhi*) to subdue the deluded mind so that it does not arise; this constitutes the non-arising of birth-and-death, which is precisely *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight).

△ "Careful examination" refers to *vipaśyanā*, meaning to scrutinize and observe with precision the various categories and proportions of beginningless deluded thoughts, knowing each one clearly—just as one must recognize a thief before being able to seize them. △ Regarding "one faculty," etc.:
As it says below: "When one faculty returns to its source, the six faculties become liberation. When all [distinctions] have vanished, the nature of awareness is fully manifest;
like ice melting and water appearing, the heavenly principle is thus revealed. Therefore it is said: "All delusions are extinguished; what need is there to wait for the unreal to cease?"

Sixth, the differentiation between the heterodox and the orthodox: When a practitioner undertakes practice, there are both correct and erroneous modes of conduct; if one does not investigate and distinguish them extensively, one will have no means of knowing which is which.
Therefore, it is necessary to identify them clearly in order to avoid deviating onto heterodox paths. Regarding those who have already awakened to the practice:

Because the Buddha has extensively revealed the various gates of practice, they have thoroughly examined the principles of cultivation. Thus, the subsequent scripture states: "I have now awakened to the Dharma-gate for accomplishing Buddhahood."
Among these, practitioners who attain freedom from doubt and the like are rare;

those of the final age, failing to be shown how to discern the truth, often fail to purify their minds with what is correct and instead follow what is deviant. Thus, Ānanda, out of compassion for the multitudes, offered this request.
△ A "leaking cup" refers to a vessel that has no bottom. △ The "four kinds of clear instructions" refer to the fundamental precepts (*mūla-śīla*). One who wishes to proceed...

Enlightenment must be attained by not transgressing in four matters; therefore, the subsequent scripture states: "When you cultivate samādhi, it fundamentally aims to escape the toils of worldly existence.

If the lustful mind is not eliminated, you cannot be liberated from the dust of defilement. Even if you possess great wisdom and dhyāna-samādhi manifests before you, if you do not sever lust, you will inevitably fall into the paths of Māra.
This is called the Tathāgata’s first definitive, pure, and clear instruction. This applies even to theft and killing.
Regarding false speech, all say this: the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time all require one to resolutely uphold these four precepts.
If the vessel of the precepts is intact, the water of concentration can be stored therein. △ "Qie" means "cautious. △ "Hong" means "vast. △ "Huan" means "to escape"; the Book of Documents says:
"When Heaven creates calamity, it may still be avoided; when one creates calamity oneself, it cannot be escaped. △ "Qiú" means "to pray for. △ "Què" means "to reject."
If one retreats and wishes to quickly reach the place previously abandoned, how could one possibly catch up?

If one wishes to swiftly arrive at the site of the fruit of Bodhi, yet halts one's steps by violating the precepts, how could one possibly reach it? Advancing forward is a metaphor for maintaining the precepts.
7. To manifest the efficacy of the mantra: As soon as the true mantra was proclaimed, Ānanda’s affliction by lust was immediately released;

how could this not be the power of the mantra? Regarding the phrase "Although he received its power," etc.: although the benefit obtained was indeed ultimate, it was such that Mañjuśrī recited it silently while Ānanda did not personally hear the words of the mantra;
thus it is said, "The secret words were lacking in hearing. It was not until the seventh fascicle that he finally returned to request [the teaching] again.
The passage following the recitation of the mantra says: "Although we have secretly obtained its power through the Tathāgata’s Buddha-Usnīṣa Divine Mantra, we have not yet heard it directly;
we pray that, out of great compassion, you will proclaim it once more. Ānanda’s request for this repetition is intended for the purpose of transmission and circulation.
As for the phrase "Moreover, [it can... and so forth, the meaning is: why must there be a repeated request for circulation? It is because this divine mantra possesses great benefit.

Through this wondrous power, the gates of the six sense faculties are closely guarded; the evil thieves of the six objects of perception can no longer enter, and the delusions of ignorance and karma may gradually be extinguished.
(The character "fáng" [防] means a dyke or embankment. The character "xián" [閑] means to ward off or restrain.

Because the seeds of beginningless habitual outflows are difficult to suppress when struck by the force of meditative concentration, one must rely on the power of mantras to provide a dyke and a defense, preventing them from destroying right practice so as to—
The active delusions are suppressed and the unarisen seeds do not arise. △ Regarding the spontaneous observance of the fast and precepts without having formally undertaken them:
this is because through the power of mantra-recitation, those who have never formally observed the fast and precepts naturally come to observe them.
Therefore, it is said below: "It can cause those who have broken the precepts to purify their roots of virtue, and cause those who have not yet attained the precepts to attain them."

It continues until it says: "Those who do not observe the fast shall observe the fast themselves," and so forth. Regarding the statement that "the realization of the fruit is not distant and can be attained," the text below says:

"After reciting and upholding my mantra for twenty-one days, an auspicious sign will appear; after sitting in *an-gu* (meditative seclusion) for one hundred days, those of sharp faculties shall attain the stage of *srotāpanna* without rising from their seats.
It further states: "One will know with certainty that the attainment of Buddhahood is unfailing."
△ Regarding those who eliminate difficulties and obtain benefit, one should know that such sentient beings who recite and uphold [this mantra] cannot be burned by fire nor drowned by water;

they cannot be harmed by great or small poisons. Furthermore, even if there are sentient beings whose minds are not in *samādhi*, yet who remember it with their hearts and maintain it with their mouths, the refined essence of Vajragarbha-rāja will swiftly manifest its spiritual sincerity in secret; such persons shall respond at that very moment.
The mind is able to remember eighty-four thousand *Ganges-sand* eons, comprehending them all-pervasively and attaining freedom from doubt;
it is further said that all the merits attained by the Tathāgatas of the ten directions are bestowed upon this person. Regarding "one's own practice," it is stated below:
"The Tathāgatas of the ten directions, by means of this dhāraṇī-heart, have attained unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment and subdued all demons."
It subdues all non-Buddhists and others. △ Regarding "transforming others," the Sūtra says: "The Tathāgatas of the ten directions contain this mantra-heart;
in lands as numerous as motes of dust, they turn the Great Dharma Wheel and can bestow empowerment upon the crown of the head and grant predictions of enlightenment throughout the ten directions.
△ Regarding "matters," these are the matters of practicing and realizing Bodhi for oneself and transforming others.
Regarding the eighth point, the stage of manifesting practice where principle transcends cultivation and realization:

since quiescent true suchness has no stages or positions, how could there be any practice to be cultivated or position to be realized? For both bodhi and nirvāṇa are like flowers in the sky. Thus, a sutra says:

"If there were even a single dharma superior to nirvāṇa, I would say that it too is like a dream or a magical illusion. And the Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra says: "Sentient beings are like [flowers in the sky]."

"The Buddhas are like grasses and trees" and so forth is spoken from the perspective of the "Gate of Extinguishing Characteristics to Reveal Reality," as stated in the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra*: "Only then does one know that sentient beings have been originally enlightened from the beginning.
And the *Treatise on the Awakening of Faith* states: "From the very beginning, they are beyond the characteristics of verbal expression and are ultimately equal.

This refers to the gate of contemplating principle to give rise to phenomena within the aspect of birth-and-death. △ As for "the existence of stages and gradual progression," this refers to the gate of contemplating principle to give rise to phenomena within the aspect of birth-and-death.
There are contemplations to be cultivated, there is bodhi and nirvana to be realized, and there are afflictions and birth-and-death to be severed;

one must pass through successive stages and gradual steps. To turn back from delusion and revolve toward the truth, one naturally traverses these stages, just as a person who studies literature and seeks office must undergo a sequence of promotions after passing the examinations. △ Regarding the sickness of being biased toward either emptiness or existence: If...
To single-mindedly cling to the absence of stages of cultivation and realization is to fall into the sickness of emptiness; as Nāgārjuna said:

"It would be better to give rise to a view of existence as large as Mount Sumeru than to give rise to a view of emptiness even as small as a mustard seed. To single-mindedly cling to existence is to fall into the view of existence;

to cling to annihilationism is to repudiate cause and effect and sever the transformation of sentient beings, resulting in the grasping of wrongly-acquired emptiness (*prāpti-śūnyatā*). To cling to permanence is to lack understanding.

The realization of the emptiness of dharmas (*dharma-śūnyatā*) fulfills the benefit [of beings], yet because the characteristics of craving and views are so remote from the cause and effect [of enlightenment], it is difficult to admit progress toward it.
△ In contrast, those who are harmonious through perfect penetration do not give rise to attachment to the two extremes; they immediately accord with the subtle principle of the Middle Way.

Because the conventional arises from the ultimate, ordinary beings and sages are not confused; thus, they compassionately rescue all classes of beings. Because the ultimate arises from the conventional, self and others are equal, such that there is no birth to be delivered.
△ Regarding "non-diminution" and so forth: this refers to the equality of quiescence and illumination. Because the essence of illumination is itself quiescence, there is no diminution;

because the essence of quiescence is itself illumination, the various stages are established. As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "Without arising from the samādhi of cessation, one manifests all majestic deportments.
The subsequent sutra states: "Arising in that very place, it is extinguished in every place," and so on. The *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* says: "That which first arises is immediately subject to extinction."

△ Regarding "knowing the occasion as the requester," the text below states: "Having thus cultivated and realized the Buddha’s samādhi, yet not having reached nirvāṇa, how is it that they are called the stage of 'dry wisdom' (śuṣka-jñāna-bhūmi)?
From what point among the forty-four minds do they gradually attain the name of 'practice,' and by reaching what locus are they said to have entered the stages (bhūmi)?
△ Regarding "teaching through practice," the Sūtra says: "At that time, the World-Honored One..."

The Honored One praised Ānanda, saying, "Excellent, excellent! You have been able to universally show to the great assembly and to all seekers of the Mahāyāna in the final age the path of supreme, correct cultivation.

Within the state of non-arising forbearance (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), you have distinguished the fifty-seven stages as distinct levels, clarifying them as the gradual steps for practice. △ Continuity.
Regarding the term "etcetera": although one cuts off delusions, there are no delusions to be cut off; only then is it true cutting off, because ignorance is itself enlightenment.
Although one realizes the stages [of attainment], there are no stages to be realized; only then is it true realization, because one has been a Buddha from the very beginning.
The "Vajra Contemplation" is the Śūraṅgama Samādhi. This samādhi is able to contemplate that all dharmas are ultimately non-existent.

One can attain that which is able to shatter all ignorance like a vajra destroying objects, such that within each and every stage, one neither severs what is not severed nor realizes what is not realized.
△ Regarding the ten similes: they are like an echo, a shadow, a mirage, the moon in water, a reflection in a mirror, empty space, a magical creation, a city of the Gandharvas, and an illusion.
△ Regarding the application of *vipaśyanā* within *śamatha*: it is the application [of insight] within [the state of] cessation.
Since it is said that contemplation proceeds through gradual and successive penetration, one knows that the stages and grounds are not non-existent.
Although they do not arise through deliberate effort but manifest spontaneously, they are like washing a garment where dirt falls away in a sequence; such is the natural order of things.
9. Showing the realms of Māra. △ "Mí" means "none. △ "Xiǎnshǎo" means "rarely few. △ "Kènéng" means "to be able to";
these are the words of the poem. This is the Tathāgata’s unasked self-exposition; it is because he deeply pities the practitioners of the final age who do not understand the true reality (dharmatā).

Fearing that they will mistakenly give rise to grasping toward what is external to this reality—whereby all else becomes the work of Māra—they would lose the correct path and fall into error; therefore, he did not wait for a request.

Because he turned his seat to speak for himself, the subsequent sutra states: "At that moment, the Tathāgata, having concluded his discourse on the Dharma-seat, turned his back upon the Purple Gold Mountain and returned to lean against his desk, universally addressing the great assembly: 'Today you have turned your minds toward Great Bodhi.
I have now already expounded the true practice, yet you still do not understand the subtle demonic affairs of practicing śamatha. [He spoke thus] so as to cause them to act."
One should clearly discern each [instance] so that neither internal nor external māras may find an opportunity; furthermore, there are three methods for discerning these māras:

first, to grind them away through meditative concentration (*samādhi*); second, to observe them with wisdom (*prajñā*); and third, to cultivate and rectify them based on the fundamental [practice]. (And so forth.)

Ten: Refuting the Source of Delusion. △ "Source" refers to the root. Although every sutra explains that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are illusory, none explicitly state that they are formed by these five kinds of deluded thoughts;
it is only in this present sutra that this is revealed most clearly. By breaking through the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), one exposes the deluded thought of solidity;

from sensation (*vedanā*), the deluded thought of empty clarity emerges; from perception (*saṃjñā*), the deluded thought of pervasive fusion emerges; and from mental formations (*saṃskāra*), the deluded thought of profound concealment emerges.
Delusory conceptualization gives rise to consciousness, which is as insubstantial and void as a phantom;

inverted conceptualization—*saṃjñā-skandha*, translated into Chinese as *yīn* (aggregate)—is so called because it obscures the true nature. *Skandha* means to accumulate, for it accumulates the conditioned afflictions.

When it arises, initial delusion forms consciousness, which ultimately culminates in form (*rūpa*); thus it is said to proceed from the subtle to the coarse. To dismantle it is the reverse process. Thus, its arising is also [the same].

Arising suddenly means there is no sense of priority or sequence; it is spoken of as "beginning and end" or "gradual severance" and also as "complete severance. It is the nature of things (*dharmatā*) that coarse defilements are eliminated first.

If it were otherwise, one would fear it would deviate from the perfect intent. However, this is merely intended to clarify the characteristics of practice, which must be manifested through a sequence even though there is no actual sequence.
Regarding the fact that the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) has no substance: failing to realize the One True Reality results in this deluded consciousness. If one investigates its...
Since the source is ultimately without substance and is entirely the single mind, Guishan said: "Consciousness is like an illusion or a dream; it is but the single mind.
Regarding "the profound entry merges with the profound": the former "profound" refers to consciousness, while the latter "profound" refers to the True [Suchness].

This means that by using meditative concentration (*samādhi*) to subdue the profound consciousness, one merges back into the principle of the tranquil profundity of True Suchness. This is precisely the limit of consciousness within True Suchness.
△ What is not included? The five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) subsume the one hundred dharmas; with the exception of the six unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharmas, all others are fully subsumed.
Thus the verse says: "The aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) subsumes eleven [dharmas] in their entirety; feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) each correspond to one [dharma];

the eight [mental factors] and the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) comprise seventy-three; the formations (*saṃskāra*) subsume the unconditioned. Because they are not accumulations and do not reside within the category of aggregates, it is known that the five aggregates subsume [all conditioned dharmas].
The conditioned is exhausted. △ This treatise refers to the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra*; its textual meaning is evident.
Regarding the classification within the two treasuries (*piṭaka*) and vehicles (*yāna*): the first treasury has already been understood through the general explanation of this sutra’s great purport;
however, it remains unknown to which of the two treasuries this sutra belongs. Therefore, it is distinguished next. In Sanskrit it is called *Kośa*, here translated as [the Treasury].
"Piṭaka" (藏) means "to contain" (*piṭ*); it is called a "piṭaka" because it can contain [the teachings]. △ The Three Piṭakas are the Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma.

In Sanskrit, *sūtra* (修多羅) is translated in the Song dynasty as "Scripture of Accordance" (*qìjīng*). This means it accords with the meaning of the Dharma and accords with the minds of sentient beings.

"Sūtra" means to thread together the explained principles so they are not lost, and to gather and sustain the capacities of those to be converted so they do not fall. Furthermore, it is "mixed" (*miśra*)...
The *Cittaviveka* (Heart Treatise) has five meanings: namely, "birth," "arousing," "measuring line," "garland," and "fountain. In Sanskrit it is called *vinaya*, which here means "discipline" (*lü*).
This refers to clarifying the rules for maintaining and violating [the precepts], much like the statutory laws of this land.

Alternatively, it is translated as "taming" (*tiaofu*), meaning to train and refine the three types of action (*trikarma*) and to subdue transgressions and faults; "training" (*tiaozhen*) applies generally to both abstention and performance, while "subduing" (*fu*) applies only to [restraint].
"Stopping evil" is alternatively translated as "cooling" (*śītalā*) or "extinguishing. In Sanskrit, it is called *abhidharma*. This term means "counter-dharma":

"dharma" refers to that which is countered (*prati*), while "abhi-" refers to that which counters (*prati-*) it. However, there are distinctions between "countering toward" (*pratimukha*) and "countering through observation" (*pratyavekṣaṇa*). If one counters reality (*tattva*) by means of ultimate wisdom (*jñāna*), it is called "countering toward";

if one counters phenomena (*vastu*) by means of subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), it is called "countering through observation. Now, among these three [meanings], [it refers to the latter].

That is to say, they are subsumed within the Sūtra-piṭaka; however, while a sūtra must necessarily expound upon the three categories [of doctrine, practice, and fruit], it receives its name based on what is predominant.

△ Second, regarding the "Pitakas": these names are established according to the persons [to whom they are addressed]. Because the first three pitakas expound the principles, practices, and fruits of the Mahāyāna, they are called the Bodhisattva-piṭaka;
because they expound the principles, practices, and fruits of the Hīnayāna, they are called the Śrāvaka-piṭaka. [This concludes the section on] Adornment.

The Treatise says: "If humans possess the three vehicles, there should accordingly be three Piṭakas; however, because the principle and the fruit of the pratyekabuddha are identical [to those of the śrāvaka], only two are established.
If one relies on the distinctions in teaching and practice, they may also be made three, and so forth.

△ If this [the present scripture] subsumes that [the other two], then the present scripture is the subsumer (the container), and the second and third [vehicles] are the subsumed (the contained). △ Regarding the observance of precepts and the realization of the fruit, there is a distinction of small [and great].
Those who have attained the third fruit, such as Aṅgīrasa, and those who have attained the second fruit, such as Ānanda, are subsumed within the Śrāvaka-piṭaka.

The four types of clear instructions are the Vinaya-piṭaka. As for the mutual refutation through debate when Ānanda was questioned and King Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta posed difficulties, this is the Abhidharma-piṭaka.

Question: Since this [Abhidharma] contains the meaning of that [Vinaya], it subsumes the latter; yet since the latter also contains the meaning of this [Abhidharma], why does it not subsume the former? Answer: Because...
This [text] can fully encompass those [teachings], whereas others can only partially encompass them; therefore, the Commentary does not discuss them.
Regarding "the One Vehicle encompassing all vehicles": this refers to the One Vehicle of the three, five, nine, and so forth.

Since the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena discussed in this sutra is the ground of quiescent extinction attained by both Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, it is exclusively the One Vehicle that encompasses this sutra.

△ Regarding "also encompassing all vehicles": the following clarifies the causes, effects, and retributions of the five precepts and ten wholesome paths, which correspond to the realms of humans and devas;
it includes the realization of the fruits by Daṅga and Ānanda, as well as the contemplation gates of the various sages—this encompasses both the Hīnayāna and the provisional Bodhisattvas.
Thus, according to the capacity of each vessel, there is no lack of benefit; even mosquitoes, gadflies, and asuras who drink its water all obtain full satisfaction.
Because they are complete, they are collectively subsumed within three divisions. △ Regarding the twelve divisions:

*nidāna* (causal conditions), *jātaka* (birth stories), *itivṛttaka* (past events), *adbhutadharma* (marvels), *avadāna* (parables), *geya* (verses following prose), *gāthā* (stanzas), *vyākaraṇa* (prophecies), *udāna* (inspired utterances), *praśnavyākaraṇa* (discussions on questions), *upadeśa* (expositions), *vaipulya* (extensive teachings), and *sūtra* (discourses).

△ Regarding the inclusion of this sutra within the Vaipulya (fangguang): "Fang" means pervasive; "guang" means great. Because this present sutra exclusively reveals that the *dharmatā* is vast, great, all-pervasive, and equal, it is thus included therein.
Furthermore, among the five names listed below, one name—*Mahāvaipulya-saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*—should be understood as the *sūtra*.
If one takes that [Vaipulya] as the category being subsumed (*saṃgrāhya*) and this sutra as the subsumer (*saṃgrāhaka*), [the relationship is established].

This thus comprehensively subsumes the twelve divisions [of the canon]: first, showing Ānanda’s encounter with the calamity of lust as the cause and the Tathāgata’s teaching as the condition constitutes the *nidāna* (causal) division;
second, the subsequent extensive elucidation of the meaning of causes and conditions constitutes the *hetu-pratyaya* (causal-condition) division;

furthermore, the five sections below are also called the *Vaipulya* (Extensive) Sūtra, which constitutes the *vaipulya* division; moreover, this single sūtra fully clarifies the meaning of the *vaipulya* of the dharma-nature.
Third, it says below: "I cause all the śrāvakas of fixed nature within your assembly to attain the ground of quiescent extinction of the One Vehicle;
although there are no designations of kalpas or lands, how can I refrain from bestowing the prediction of Buddhahood? This is the section on the Bestowal of Predictions. Fourth, it says below:
"The Tathāgata, about to leave the Dharma-seat, again leans upon his armrest and addresses the great assembly: 'You still do not recognize [the state] within śamatha...'"
The section on subtle demonic activities (*sūkṣma-māra-karman*) and so forth is the "Unasked Spontaneous Exposition" (*apṛṣṭa-vyākaraṇa*), the fifth [division].

It says below: "I am now like a traveler who has suddenly been granted a magnificent mansion by the Heavenly King; one must enter through the gate. Within a single sūtra, there are numerous parables which cannot be recorded in full;
this is the "Parable Section" (*avadāna*), the sixth. Furthermore, below it says: "King Prasenajit posed a difficult question, and Ānanda [responded] again..."

The section on "Refuting the Causes and Conditions" (責因緣) consists of seven parts that investigate the location of the mind and resolve disputes through three doubts; this is the "Section on Doctrinal Discussion" (論義分). The seventh part states:
"The Wondrously Profound, All-Holding, Immovable Honored One, the King of Śūraṅgama, is rare in the world.

Furthermore, it says: "We have not previously heard of the five aggregates and the five delusions forming one another"; this is the "Section on the Unprecedented" (未曾有分). The eighth part clarifies the long-standing attachment of Mātanga across kalpas.
The *Vinayavibhaṅga* further recounts the past deeds of the twenty-five holy ones; it also states that these are no different from [the accounts of] my own period of eating horse-barley and so forth.

Furthermore, the ninth section of the *Mūlavastu* states: "Recalling one's own births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges" refers to the *Jātaka-vastu*, which describes the past lives of the Buddha and his disciples.
Describing the past lives of the Buddha and his disciples is called the *Itivṛttaka*. Describing the past lives of the Buddha and his disciples... [is called the *Nidāna*].

Regarding the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra*, the section on the "Ten Births" (*daśa-jāti*) states: "For example, if a person is dwelling in stillness and drums are struck simultaneously in the ten directions, they hear them all at once in those ten places.

This refers to the *Gāthā* (verse) portion. The section on the "Eleven [Verses]" states: "How wonderful is Avalokiteśvara! Entering into Buddha-lands as numerous as motes of dust, he has attained the power of great mastery.
This refers to the *Ge-yā* (verse) portion. As for the twelfth, the *Sūtra* (prose), it is as explained in the regular [commentaries]. Thus it is said.
The summary of these is as before.

Regarding the second section, "The Distinction between the Teachings and Their Meanings," there are two parts. First, the headings: the teaching is the means of expression (*vācaka*), and the meaning is that which is expressed (*vācya*).

Now, the superiority or inferiority of the teaching as the means of expression is determined by the depth or shallowness of the meaning it expresses. △ "Worthy Chief" (*Xianxiu*) refers to the *Avataṃsaka* [Sūtra].

After the passing of the Master Zongzhi, he was posthumously honored with the title "Great Master Xianshou" by imperial decree. **II. Correctly Distinguishing [the Teachings]** The first section concerns the scope and limitations of the teachings as they express the Dharma;
it clarifies the boundaries [of these teachings]. **A. The General Scope and Limitations** This section first provides the heading. Regarding "scope and limitations":

"general" refers to the three teachings of the Final, Sudden, and Perfect [Vehicles], because they are vast and inclusive, because they extensively accommodate the capacities of sentient beings, and because they express profound meanings and reveal the ultimate principle.
Because it is real, it destroys delusions; because it is subtle, it is fresh and perfect; because it is sudden, it is equal from beginning to end;

and because it is restricted, it pertains to the Hīnayāna and the Initial Teaching (*śaikṣa*). Because its expressed meaning is shallow, the capacity of those it addresses is narrow, and its understanding is not perfectly integrated.

Furthermore, since the profound must necessarily encompass the shallow, while that which encompasses the shallow does not necessarily include the profound, it is "restricted. Alternatively, the latter four teachings may be considered "universal," whereas the ignorant Hīnayāna is "restricted."
Section: △ "Teaching" (Jiao) means instruction. It refers to the words spoken by the Sage for those below him; it instructs the ordinary to become sages and the ignorant to become wise.
First is the Teaching of the Hīnayāna. △ Regarding "Hīnayāna": because it carries those of small capacity to a small fruit, it is called the Small Vehicle. What is the meaning [of this]?
One must explain that it was the "Lesser" [Vehicle]. For when a Sage expounds the teachings, it is for the purpose of delivering sentient beings according to their capacities;

if the teaching were not adapted to their capacities, what benefit would there be? Furthermore, if one were to preach only the profound [teachings], those who slander them would fall into evil realms.

Therefore, while the Tathāgata remained unmoved at the site of tranquility, he traveled to the Deer Park and, for twelve years, taught and guided them by means of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) Dharma. This is merely for the sake of those people of deluded capacity.

Having attained the realization of non-self, one may still not yet know that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are empty in their very essence—just as when a fist is dismantled, the five fingers remain.
Nevertheless, according to the sutras and śāstras, this [teaching] also refutes attachment to phenomena within the realm of desire (*dhātu*), and so forth.

△ It is said that those who speak only of the emptiness of self (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) are all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who cling to the mark of a self and grasp at all phenomena as belonging to a self; therefore, this teaching refutes [such views].

If one asserts that there is a self because of the existence of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), then there should be many selves, just as a single aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) consists of ten types of matter;
thus, there would have to be eleven types of self. By conducting such an investigation, one knows that there is no self.
