III. Briefly Explaining the Roots for Cultivation and Realization: First, a General Exhortation to Careful Discernment. △ Regarding "tracing back to the root of the outflows" (*liú-gēn*):

tracing back to the very root of the outflows of desire refers to the wondrous principle of the Three Truths, which is the root of the outflows; alternatively, it refers to the meaning of the "True Outflow" (*zhēn-liú*), which encompasses both the shallow and the deep, while the "root" (*gēn*) refers exclusively to the ultimate.
△ Regarding the "six roots of enjoyment" (*shòu-yòng-gēn*): these refer to the reception and grasping of the six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*) and the subsequent formative activities (*abhisamskāra*).
This concerns the karma of good and evil. △ As for "conjunction," it means that one must perceive through the conjunction of the object and the sense faculty;
the three faculties of nose, tongue, and body both perceive through conjunction. Eye, ear, and mind—these three perceive through non-conjunction.

△ "Deep" refers to the mental faculty (*manas*), as its creation of karma is the deepest. △ "Shallow" refers to the first five [faculties]: eye, nose, and body, which are not considered perfectly penetrating (*pariśuddha*), according to the analysis by Mañjuśrī in the following text.
This briefly indicates that the ear-faculty (*śrotra-indriya*) alone is the perfect means of penetration (*āyatana*). ▲ Second, specifically demonstrating its functional power.
△ "The weaving of delusory karma-flow" refers to the interweaving of emptiness and the faculty of vision, which binds together the sense-bases and their objects to create delusory karma.

△ "Days and kalpas multiply each other" means that practicing with the perfect faculty for a single day is superior to practicing with an imperfect faculty for an entire kalpa. ▲ Third, granting permission to clarify and manifest [the truth]. △ Six.
"Profound, perfect, and luminous" refers to the fundamental source; it means that based on one pure, brilliant essence, the six harmonious aggregates are differentiated.

△ "Revealing and clarifying" means that according to whichever faculty you desire, I shall for your sake develop and clearly manifest it, so that you may take it as a rule for cultivation and attain the supreme fruit.
▲ Fourth, one must distinguish the underlying reasons. △ By practicing each [faculty] individually, all shall attain perfection.

As for "fulfillment," through the cultivation of wondrous wisdom, there is nothing that cannot be realized; why then would one need to make further distinctions? As it says below: "Both following and reversing are expedient means.

Regarding "sovereign wisdom," this is the wisdom of the true mark (*dharmatā*). This wisdom illuminates all phenomena such that nothing is not truly real, and because it is not obstructed by things, it is called "sovereign.
At the beginning of the petition, Ānanda’s underlying intention was to ask: if the six sense faculties are truly of one essence, [how is it that they function differently?]
Furthermore, there are differences regarding the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya*). If the six entities were distinct, how could they enter into one?

If even this is so, how much more so for those who have not yet abandoned attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*)! *Srotāpanna* (須陀洹) here means "逆流" (逆流, *praty-anusrota*), referring to the first fruit, which involves the severance of the eighty-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*) of the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-heya*).
"Severed by seeing" (*darśana-heya*) refers to that which is severed within the gateway of the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*). "Severed by cultivation" (*bhāvanā-heya*)... [text continues]

"Severed" refers to the innate delusions (*sahaja-kleśa*) that are abandoned within the gateway of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). The phrase "how much more so" (*kaḥ punar vādaḥ*) constitutes the formal analogy:

if even the afflictions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya-kleśa*) remain within the faculties of one's own vehicle (*svayāna*), how much more so the extent and quantity of the fundamental ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*) within these very faculties?

Arising, abiding, change, and cessation are the subtle delusions of failing to realize the nature of the single Dharma-realm (*ekadharmadhātu-svabhāva*). To say "six" or "one" is itself subtle [delusion].
The first refutation of attachment to subtle dharmas. △ This is the practice of fulfillment. △ "What" (xi) means "how" (he). ▲ The three fetters.
△ "Not one, ending in six" means discarding one while retaining six. △ "Not six, ending in one" means discarding six while retaining one.

Only when both one and six are discarded is it the ultimate teaching; for within the nature of perfect permanence, there is fundamentally neither one nor six. Therefore, it is said: "Ultimately not..."

This merely negates the existence of objects while distinguishing the mind from non-existence; it does not mean that the mind itself is non-existent. All phenomena are manifested solely by the mind;
apart from the mind, no characteristics of external objects exist. If one realizes that there are no phenomena outside the mind, then the frantic pursuit [of external things] will naturally vanish.

Regarding the name "Mahāsthāmaprāpta" (Great Power Attained), the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states: "I vow that my world shall be no different from that of Avalokiteśvara. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-upadeśa* states:

"The place where I set foot causes the great trichiliocosm and the palaces of Māra to tremble; thus I am named Mahāsthāmaprāpta. (Because his power takes hold of the world without contradicting his resolve, he is named "World-Resolve.

△ "Not interrupted by thoughts" means there is no separation caused by deviant thoughts; this is what the Sūtra refers to when it says, "with single-mindedness, without confusion.

Fifth, Avalokiteśvara. △ Regarding "returning the hearing to the reality": this means returning the faculty of hearing to observe its own nature in order to realize the true mark.
This intention reveals that while the practices of other sages mostly enter through provisional means, only this gate allows one to practice the perfect and real from the very beginning.
Now, as for why Avalokiteśvara is mentioned last, there are three reasons: first, because the meaning of "perfect penetration" (yuan-tong) is broad.

It is precisely because of this expedient suitability that the gates of cultivation and realization are fully revealed, and the characteristics of the ritual procedures for transformation are extensively expounded.

Second, regarding the aspect of the succession of celebratory discourse: the intention is that immediately after Avalokiteśvara’s teaching, there should be a celebration and praise, thereby expressing that while the primary praise is directed at Avalokiteśvara, it also incidentally encompasses the other sages.
If the teaching were given next to Kātyāyanīputra (Nalü) without such celebration, the excellence of Avalokiteśvara would not be manifested.

If one were to praise [the Buddha] as supreme immediately after [his appearance], then it would follow that the subsequent teachings of the various sages were not intentionally reserved for later exposition;
thus, the praise itself would naturally imply the primary and secondary [teachings]. Third, regarding the "Instruction on the Continuous Avalokiteśvara":

having finished the exposition, he then commanded Mañjuśrī to analyze the matter of the continuous succession so that the teaching would never be interrupted. When first encountering the Buddha, he received the instruction; in Sanskrit, this is called *Abhilaṣita*.

*Kiṭiśvarā* (Cīdìshìfúluó) is translated here as Guanzizai (Avalokiteśvara). The Tripiṭaka Master of the Tang dynasty explained it as "observing existence without dwelling in existence, and observing emptiness without dwelling in emptiness.
Hearing his name, one is not deluded by the name; seeing his form, one is not submerged in the form. The mind cannot be moved, and the environment cannot cause movement to follow.
Even when following along with circumstances, he is not disordered from the truth. He may truly be called one possessed of unimpeded wisdom. This is the complete [explanation].
"Being able to contemplate" is what constitutes the name "Avalokiteśvara"; this is a designation that combines both the subject and the object.
"Contemplation" (*guan*) refers to the subject—the three types of contemplation—while "Avalokiteśvara" refers to the objects—the sounds of all three types of worlds.

Because wondrous wisdom contemplates these [objects] such that they are none other than emptiness, the provisional, and the middle, it is said that the name is established based on the relationship between the subject and object, and the environment and wisdom. Tiantai says: "Subject and object..."

The perfect interfusion of existence and non-existence allows for the simultaneous and thorough illumination and penetration of the true nature; by examining both its root and its branches, he is called Avalokiteśvara.
His own practice has achieved manifest merit, and his transformation of others is certain. The sufferings of the ten realms can all be universally rescued by the Bodhisattva’s vast compassion.

This constitutes both his self-cultivation and his transformation of others, both of which are Avalokiteśvara. As the *Mahākaruṇā Sūtra* states: "In the past, he attained Buddhahood under the name of Samyag-dharma."
The *Sūtra on the Prediction of the Tathāgata* states that [Avalokiteśvara] will succeed Maitreya in the place of Amitābha;

yet whether this is provisional or ultimate, whether it pertains to the fundamental or the manifested, none can know for certain. △ All those whom he took as teachers—the Buddhas he encountered—and all the contemplations he practiced were centered upon Avalokiteśvara.

"Listening, etc. refers to the second [stage]: practicing contemplation according to the teachings. Regarding "first, within listening": this refers to the initial hearing of the verbal teachings. Regarding "entering the stream":

this means not following the verbal teachings, but rather penetrating the principle through the essence of the words and turning back to contemplate the nature of hearing itself. Regarding "that which is entered is already tranquil": that which is...

Because the principle realized is fundamentally profound stillness, the two characteristics of external objects—movement and stillness—cannot be apprehended; therefore, it is said that "it is clearly non-arising.
"Where hearing and what is heard are both exhausted": since movement and stillness no longer exist, the nature of movement and stillness that perceives them is also exhausted.
Following this exhaustion, one does not dwell in or cling to the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*). "The awareness and what is aware are empty": this refers to the subject that is aware.
The awakening of the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) is also non-existent; that which is the awakening of the wisdom of hearing is precisely the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*).

△ Regarding "the awakening of emptiness is perfectly complete": emptiness is the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*), and awakening is the wisdom of reflection. △ Regarding "that which is emptied and the emptiness itself are extinguished": the subject that empties is the wisdom of cultivation, and the object emptied is the sphere of the wisdom of reflection; these two are extinguished simultaneously.
All three types of wisdom are utterly extinguished: through hearing, words vanish as one penetrates the principle; through reflection, both words and the principle vanish together;

and through cultivation, object and wisdom are simultaneously extinguished. Thus, one realizes non-arising. Therefore it is said: "When birth and death are extinguished, quiescent extinction manifests.

If we discuss the stages, hearing corresponds to the stage of names; contemplative practice corresponds to the stage of Avalokiteśvara; and reflection and cultivation correspond to the stage of semblance-Avalokiteśvara, which is quiescent extinction.
Regarding the passage in the *Avalokiteśvara Commentary* beginning with "The manifestation is itself the partial and ultimate [realization]":

Birth brings liberation from suffering and the attainment of bliss; thus, that which manifests should not be divorced from the two bodies, the Real and the Responsive.

Although they first attained self-awakening, its fulfillment must necessarily rely on guidance to bring it to completion; thus, there is no contradiction. If they encounter the appearance of a Buddha, they will undergo transformation through fire, incinerating their bodies and entering Nirvana.

▲ Third, the Pratyekabuddhas. △ Regarding "the excellence of severing conditions": the severance of the twelve links of dependent origination is precisely the realization of true nature (*tathatā*).

△ The process of transmigration and cessation is as previously explained. △ Taking "origination" (*samudaya*) as the primary gateway means first contemplating ignorance; this is precisely the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*).
The foremost śrāvaka takes the Truth of Suffering as the primary gateway; the twelve links of dependent origination are likewise the Four Noble Truths.

Ignorance, volitional formations, craving, grasping, and becoming constitute the Truth of Origination; consciousness, name-and-form, and so forth constitute the Truth of Suffering; the wisdom capable of contemplation constitutes the Truth of the Path;

and the principle realized constitutes the Truth of Cessation. Regarding the pratyekabuddha: "dependent" refers to the twelve links of dependent origination, and "enlightened" refers to awakening through the oral teachings.

This is precisely the wisdom of awakening. ▲ Fourth, the Śrāvakas. △ Regarding the "contracted contemplation" (saṃkṣipta-vipaśyanā) of the Four Noble Truths: this refers to the contaminated contracted contemplation of the Four Noble Truths.

It means that one first contemplates the Four Noble Truths—suffering, origin, cessation, and the path—of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), with each truth possessing four aspects (*ākāra*), thus forming sixteen aspects.
[Then] one causes the contemplation of the two higher realms to likewise possess sixteen aspects, thereby completing thirty-two aspects in total.

"Contraction" means gradually observing and gradually contracting so that the object of observation becomes narrow. This occurs during the stage of "Middle Patience" (*madhyakṣānti*), wherein one performs seven cycles of reducing the objects (*ālambana*) and twelve cycles of reducing the aspects (*ākāra*).
First, one contemplates the aspects of suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self (*anātman*) regarding the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) of the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*);

next, one contemplates the same for the Higher Realms (*ūrdhvadhātu*). Then, one contemplates the Truth of Origination (*samudayasatya*) of the Desire Realm as origination, cause, condition, and production; next, one contemplates the same for the Higher Realms.

The same applies to the origin and cessation truths of the realms (*dhātu*). Furthermore, one contemplates the cessation, tranquility, excellence, and renunciation of the cessation truth of the desire realm;

one then contemplates the upper realms in the same way. Again, one contemplates the path, method, practice, and emergence of the path truth of the desire realm; one then contemplates the upper realms in the same way.
However, regarding the path truth of the upper realms, one contemplates only the path, method, and practice, and does not contemplate the single aspect of "emergence. This is the first [section].
In this manner, one row is gradually reduced until only a single object—the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) within the desire realm—remains (and so forth).

Regarding the sixteen moments of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*): within this realization of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*), these sixteen moments consist of eight patiences (*kṣānti*) and eight knowledges (*jñāna*), namely:

the patience of the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*), the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñāna*), the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe ’nvayajñānakṣānti*), the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe ’nvayajñāna*), and the patience of the dharma-knowledge of origin (*samudaye dharmajñānakṣānti*).

The sixteen moments of mind are: the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of origin (*samudaya-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*), the subsequent knowledge of origin (*anvaya-jñāna*); the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*), the dharma-knowledge of cessation (*dharma-jñāna*), the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*), and the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*anvaya-jñāna*); the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of the path (*mārga-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*), the dharma-knowledge of the path (*dharma-jñāna*), the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of the path (*anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*), and the subsequent knowledge of the path (*anvaya-jñāna*).
These sixteen moments involve one receptivity and one knowledge for each of the four truths of the desire realm; the same applies when observing the two higher realms collectively.

When each of the one patience (*kṣānti*) and one knowledge (*jñāna*) reaches the level of the Truth of the Path, one further patience arises, termed the fifteenth moment of mind; subsequently, one knowledge arises, termed the sixteenth moment of mind.
At this point, the delusions of vision (*darśana-heya-kleśa*) are completely exhausted all at once, and one realizes the first fruit (*phala*).

Second, the section on the counterparts of Śakra and Brahmā. △ Regarding the entry into and emergence from the factors of dhyāna (*dhyānāṅga*): one emerges from one [level] and enters another, practicing them in successive order;
each dhyāna possesses a multitude of constituent qualities (*aṅga-vana-guṇa*). *Brahmā* is called *Trāyastriṃśa* in Sanskrit, which translates as "Thirty-three.

Śakra-devānām-indra is translated as "The Lord of the Thirty-three" because he is able to act as the sovereign of the thirty-three heavens; he is also translated as "The Capable Heavenly Emperor. *Yāma* is also called *Suyāma*.

*Maṇi* is translated here as "Time" (*kāla*) or "Exquisite" (*sādhu*). *Tuṣita* is translated as "Contentment. In Sanskrit, *Suyāma* is translated as "Delighting in Emanation," which refers to the Heaven of the Sovereign Gods.
In Sanskrit, *Vaśavartin* is translated as "Mastery over Others' Emanations. Regarding "delighting in one's own emanations" and "delighting in others' emanations":
"delighting in one's own" refers to the Heaven of Delighting in Emanation, where one delights in one's own superior emanations.
Delighting in things and enjoying the transformations of others refers to the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, where one enjoys the transformations produced by others.

One is entangled by worldly affairs; the four evil realms abound in suffering, leaving no leisure for spiritual cultivation. Only among humans is there what is called "happiness," for humans are those who cultivate themselves.

Regarding the first of the fourteen fearlessnesses: upon first hearing the sound, one is freed from suffering. As for not contemplating oneself as the Avalokiteśvara, it is because one is able [to do so] through one's own self-power.

Because Avalokiteśvara observes the nature of hearing by turning back to observe his own sound, it is said, "using observation to observe. Here, the second instance of the character "observe" (guān) refers precisely to the nature of hearing.
Since he has realized this for himself, he causes others to observe as well, so that all may attain liberation.

Furthermore, the reason he does not merely "observe the sounds" is that, through the Samādhi of the Wondrous Sound of the World (*Lengyan Miaoding*), he uses his contemplative illumination to observe all sounds within the Dharma-realm; these sounds do not arise from himself.

It is not born from itself, not born from another, not born from both, nor does it arise without cause. Here, I briefly cite the single phrase "not born from itself" to encompass the latter three phrases.
By investigating through these four points, one finds that sound has no place of birth; one perceives only the auditory nature, which is fundamentally pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm.
Therefore, it is said: "By means of contemplation, one contemplates. Regarding this, Gushan says: "Because I do not contemplate my own ears. This is because...
When I extinguish the dust, it merges with the nature; having personally realized this nature, I immediately give rise to the transformation of others.

Because I constantly contemplate the sentient beings who hear sounds within the ten dharma realms, it is said: "By means of contemplation, one contemplates. Regarding the first point, "the three calamities in evil lands":

as for "knowing-seeing revolving and subduing," it is because through contemplating the nature of hearing, one silently accords with the true principle, and the other faculties likewise revolve; therefore, it is called "knowing-seeing."
Turning back to what was said below: "If one place achieves rest and restoration, the six functions will all cease. Regarding "fire does not burn":
when knowledge and vision illuminate and discern, they are like the brilliant radiance of fire. Now, since knowledge and vision have been restored, fire does not burn.

Furthermore, seeing can manifest anger, and anger gives rise to fire; because knowledge and vision are restored, fire spontaneously does not arise. Thus, even the fires of sensory objects cannot affect it.

This burning is explained here according to the faculties [of the practitioners] for the sake of practical convenience; however, there are three kinds of fire: first, the fire of karmic retribution; second, the fire of karma;
and third, the fire of afflictions (*kleśa*). The fire of retribution extends from the hells up to the First Dhyāna; the fire of karma pervades the three realms. As the Sūtra says:

"There is no burning of the roots of goodness that exceeds anger. These afflictions begin with ordinary beings and extend all the way to the Stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-sambodhi*) in the Perfect Teaching.
The fires of the afflictions of the five stages of abiding are likewise entirely liberated through the power of the Bodhisattva.

When wisdom arises and the essence of mind is clearly manifested, it is called the Stage of Resolving Mind (*cittotpāda-vihāra*). Regarding this "resolving mind," it refers to the arising of three types of mind:

first, the manifestation of the nature of the direct cause, which is the arising of the mind of principle (*li-xin*); second, the direct cause as wisdom, which is the arising of the mind of knowledge (*zhi-xin*);

and third, the contributory cause as practice, which is the arising of the mind of conduct (*xing-xin*). When these ten kinds of triads manifest simultaneously, one dwells without dwelling; this is dwelling in the inconceivable liberation.
It is not only by being liberated from this state that the three minds are developed; rather, as soon as ignorance is shattered and principle is seen, the three minds are immediately developed.
(2) Regarding "the mind illuminates and clarifies," this refers back to the preceding point; "illuminates and clarifies" means to manifest.
"Treading upon it to form the ground" means taking this very mind as the foundation and relying upon it to manifest wondrous function. "Ground" carries the sense of being able to produce.
Therefore, because the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) serves as the object of observation for the second stage, it is called the "Stage of Preparing the Ground" (*kṣānti-bhūmi*).
Alternatively, it may be understood that within the lapis lazuli-like void, the semblance of refined gold appears. (3) △ Regarding "traversing the ten directions":

this means that through the union of principle and wisdom (*jñāna*), one is able to give rise to great function. (4) Regarding "conduct being of the same category as the Buddha": this means that true wisdom is identical to the ultimate fruit. △
Those who receive a portion of the Buddha’s breath are those who partially realize and ultimately equalize the principle;
having already conformed with the Buddha’s wisdom and principle, they take the two wisdoms of provisional and ultimate as their parents, just as a physical body seeks its own parents.
△ Regarding "entering the lineage of the Tathāgata": having conformed with the Buddha’s two wisdoms, one receives the Buddha’s legacy-body, first entrusting oneself to the holy embryo.
The lineage of the Buddhas is never severed. [Section] Five. △ Those who personally receive the legacy of the Awakened One thereby inherit his vital energy as their seed;

thus they are nurtured and raised until all practices are perfected. This is like a person in the womb who possesses all five stages of development; therefore, it is said that "the human characteristics are not deficient."
▲ Six. △ One whose appearance is like that of a Buddha is fully endowed with wisdom and principle, as well as unconditioned compassion;

Although they are thus perfectly interfused, the sequence of stages remains distinct, with their high and low levels never being confused.

The four stages of application (*prayoga*). *Commentary:* Regarding the five stages of the Hīnayāna: the five stages of settling the mind (*pañca-vasthā-citta-sthiti*) and the general and specific applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) are termed the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*).

The stages of Heat (*uṣmagata*), Peak (*mūrdhan*), Patience (*kṣānti*), and the First World (*laukikāgra-dharma*) are termed the first stage of application (*prayoga-avasthā*). The first fruit (*phala*) is the stage of penetration (*prativedha-avasthā*), while the second and third fruits are [the stages of cultivation].

The stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-avasthā*) is designated as the four fruits, while the stage of culmination (*niṣṭhā-avasthā*) is designated as such. △ In the Mahāyāna *lakṣaṇa-vāda* (Dharma-character) school, the three levels of worthiness (*tri-kalyāṇa*) are termed the outer ordinary beings (*bāhyapṛthagjana*), the stage of provisions (*sambhāra-avasthā*);
the four stages of application (*catasraḥ prayogabhūmayaḥ*) are termed the inner ordinary beings (*adhyātmapṛthagjana*), the stage of application (*prayoga-avasthā*);

the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) is termed the stage of penetration (*prativedha-avasthā*); from the second stage onward is termed the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-avasthā*); and wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) is termed the stage of culmination (*niṣṭhā-avasthā*). However, the present position is situated after the stage of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).
Upon entering the first stage (*bhūmi*), one performs these four types of applied effort (*prayoga*) to destroy the obstacles to entering the first stage;
there may be those who do not [attain it], which includes the dedication (*pariṇāmana*) and the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*) within the stages. Question:

From the preceding section up to this point, those of sharp faculties have already destroyed forty-one grades of ignorance (*avidyā*), while those of slightly duller faculties destroy thirty grades. How much more so, then, is this the case for those who apply effort? Answer: All... [text ends]
The sūtras, śāstras, and the Dharma-lakṣaṇa school all maintain that the first bhūmi is the entry into principle;

because it is difficult to enter this principle for the first time, they describe four types of preparatory practice (*prayoga*). In the Perfect and Real Teaching (*yuanshi jiao*), however, there are no stages to be discussed;

rather, one provisionally employs the terminology of the provisional teachings to distinguish the sequence of stages within the Perfect [Teaching], and thus these are established as being prior to the bhūmis. Although the names are the same as those of the provisional, their meaning must be Perfect and Real.
The *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* states: "The three levels of the worthy and the ten stages of the sages abide in retributive fruit; only the Buddha alone dwells in the Pure Land.
Nevertheless, four preparatory practices (*prayoga*) are established prior to the [first] stage (*bhūmi*). There are three reasons for this: first, they are established as provisional expedients;

second, because the heights and depths of the [actual] stages are so profound, it is difficult to advance further, making them distinct from the preceding levels where the destruction of attachments was still shallow—just as when a person passes the imperial examination and becomes an official, they must still pass through successive appointments.

Although many will enter the temple hall (the state of sagehood), it is even more appropriate to further advance in virtue and cultivate one's practice. Thirdly, this also encompasses the distinct capacities [of various practitioners];

by entering through cultivation at this stage, there is the principle of "repeated application" following the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Because these three intentions exist, it appears prior to the stages (*bhūmi*).
The first stage is called "Ultimate Determination," and the final stage is called "Liberation. Although the initial mind aspires toward the ultimate, and...

△ To take the Buddha’s awakening as one's own mind means to employ the resultant wisdom (*phala-jñāna*) of the First Ground as one's own causal mind.

Regarding the mutual relationship between the stages of fruition (*phala-avasthā*), cause and effect are discussed in terms of their coexistence as two aspects.
△ As for the identity of mind and Buddha, this refers to the equality of cause and effect; because the "middle aspect" still persists, it is said that one has not yet transcended consciousness-only.

To establish even a slight object before oneself and claim it is the nature of consciousness-only is to have something apprehended; therefore, one does not truly abide in consciousness-only. △ Delusion and Awakening.

That which is called "cause and effect" is the deluded perception of cause and effect. △ Regarding the previous two stages, it is said that they rely on the two concentrations of *ālokalabdha* (attainment of light) and *vṛddhāloka* (increase of light).

Relying on the concentration of *ālokalabdha*, one gives rise to the lower levels of vitarka and vicāra; by contemplating the four dharmas—the name, the object, the self-nature of name and object, and the distinctions of name and object—one establishes that the grasped (*grāhya*) is non-existent.
This constitutes the stage of *uṣmagata* (Heat), because these four dharmas are all [of the nature of] self-... [text truncated].

The mind is provisionally established as existing (initially attaining the name "clarity" when wisdom-sun arises, this is the Samādhi of Attaining Clarity). "Investigation and analysis" (*vitarka-vicāra*) refer to seeking and examining;

that is, the four dharmas named investigation, analysis, and so forth, exist only nominally and lack substantial reality. Based on the Samādhi of Increasing Clarity, one gives rise to superior investigation and analysis to repeatedly contemplate that there is nothing to be grasped;

this is the stage of the "Summit" (*mūrdhan*), wherein one repeatedly contemplates that the four dharmas cannot be found to have any real existence (the aspect of clarity increases further, hence it is called the Samādhi of Increasing Clarity). △ [End of section] Afterward...
The two [kinds of] individuals, relying on the *mudrā-anuloma-samādhi*, give rise to the lower *yathābhūta-jñāna*;

they definitively seal and uphold the absence of the apprehended (*grāhya*), and regarding the absence of the apprehender (*grāhaka*), they likewise accord with *kṣānti*. This is established as the stage of *kṣānti*.

That is, having sealed the former and conformed to the latter, relying on the *anantarya-samādhi*, they give rise to the higher *yathābhūta-jñāna*, sealing both apprehended and apprehender as empty; this is called the "Supreme Worldly Dharma" (*laukikāgra-dharma*). Immediately following this—

One who necessarily enters the Path of Seeing is called "uninterrupted" (*ānantarya*). However, the contemplative gates established in the four aforementioned stages are all practices cultivated prior to realization;
now, in this stage of realization, one cultivates concentration and wisdom in their entirety, entering gradually and deepening progressively.
The seventy stages: first, the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*). △ "Stage" (*bhūmi*) carries the meaning of that which can be traversed, as well as the meaning of giving birth.

this refers to the profound union of wondrous wisdom with the principle of the fruit. At such a time, one is far removed from conceptual discrimination and agitation; the aspects of subject and object are stilled and separated.

Because one opens the gate of illumination of the hundred dharmas and realizes the secret treasury of the three virtues amidst the five fears, it is called "thorough penetration" (*suvicita*) and also the "Stage of the Only Son.
Because one has already departed from the obstacle of the nature of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), one regards all sentient beings equally as if they were one's only son.

Regarding the predominance of *dāna-pāramitā* (the perfection of giving): this indicates that while the Bodhisattva of this stage also cultivates all the perfections, it is specifically emphasized because of its superior development.
It is called "entering this stage" because at this time, the three—principle, wisdom, and practice—as well as the various *dhāraṇīs* and so forth, are simultaneously manifested.
Regarding "pervasive practice": True Suchness (*tathatā*) pervades all phenomena of flux; now, one realizes that birth-and-death and coming-and-going are fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha.

It represents the causes and effects of birth within the six realms of existence. The "three realms and nine stages" consist of the five realms of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the four dhyānas of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and the four spheres of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
"To cause birth intentionally" means to give rise to the afflictions of craving and attachment (*tṛṣṇā-kleśa*) which moisten and sustain rebirth.
This refers to the teaching and transformation of sentient beings within the three realms.

Regarding the second section, the summary and demonstration: "Those who rely on the preceding and succeeding [stages] to assist one another" means that when the conventional is identical to the ultimate, all things are utterly extinguished;
yet when the ultimate is identical to the conventional, cause and effect are clearly manifest. To remain fixed in either side exclusively results in the views of annihilationism or eternalism.
First, the general division into two parts: one, the enumeration of headings. △ Regarding the phrase "due to that deluded vision, deluded habit-energies arise":

sentient beings’ false discrimination gives rise to the notion of a Buddha and a world-world. As the *Awakening of Faith* states: "All phenomena exist with their distinctions solely based on deluded thought.
Since they are created by delusion, they must be subject to deluded attachment. As the *Saddharma-smṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states: "It is like a rope binding a flying [bird]."
Just as a bird, though far away, returns when summoned, so too should one know that sentient beings, though drawn by their karma, can likewise return.
Second, the perception of external factors (*bāhya-aṅga-saṃjñā*) enables one to fly upward; even until the attainment of Buddhahood, one relies upon mental conceptualization (*saṃjñā-manasikāra*).

This is like the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra*, where one contemplates Amitābha and is thereby born in the Pure Land. However, "internal factors" (*antaraṅga*) does not mean the absence of perception (*asaṃjñā*); rather, it refers to perceptions that are tainted by emotional defilement (*kleśa*).
Furthermore:

First, within the state of pure thought (*cintā*), △ the opening of the mind and the vision of the Buddha must also be understood as encompassing the stages of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*) and semblance-realization (*sādṛśya-bhūmi*) (and so forth).
▲ Second, when emotion is slight and thought is predominant, △ the causes for differentiation—such as the superior, middling, and inferior grades—are as explained above.
As explained in the section on the deeds of Māra: △ The four classes of celestial seers and ghosts have nine modes of perception; the powerful spirits and deities have eight modes of perception;
the flying yakṣas have seven modes of perception; and the earth-walking rākṣasas have six modes of perception. △ Regarding the "Dharmakṣānti of Universal Retention":

it means to maintain and preserve [the Dharma] in peace and security so that there is no regression. ▲ Three. △ Regarding "when thought and perception are equalized" and "one who is clear-minded and intelligent": here, "perception" (saṃjñā) refers to...
The *dharma* of clarity (*prabhāsvara*), if slightly increased, necessarily results in intelligence; the *dharma* of darkness (*tamas*), if slightly increased, necessarily results in dullness.
[Note: There are many types of the four afflictions. Regarding "Avīci": the *Abhidharmakośa* states that among the seven hot hells, the eighth is named Avīci;
however, apart from these eight hot hells, there are five distinct Avīci hells of their own.

The three fetters arise from one's own karma. Regarding the "mutual transformation within the mutual" (the shared aspect of the collective), mountains, rivers, the great earth, the hells, and so forth, are the *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) resulting from the collective karma of sentient beings.
This involves four propositions: first, the mutual transformation within the mutual, such as mountains, rivers, and the hells;

second, the non-mutual within the mutual, such as fields, gardens, and property; third, the mutual within the non-mutual, such as wives and daughters; [and fourth, the non-mutual within the non-mutual].
Among the four types of non-common [retributions], "non-common" refers specifically to the *sambhogakāya* (body of perfect enjoyment).

"Experiencing this suffering together" means that various beings collectively undergo the same sufferings, such as being boiled in cauldrons. "Experiencing retribution differently" means that although they are equally reborn in hell, the specific sufferings they endure differ;
for instance, one may be on an iron bed while another is on a mountain of knives, or one is in the eight cold hells while another is in the eight hot hells. "The original ground" refers to...
This means that the very causes one originally created—such as iron balls—result in the experience of suffering from those same iron balls, thereby linking the preceding life to the subsequent one.

Regarding "projecting" and "fulfilling": that which draws one into hell is the projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karma*); the experience of its varying degrees of severity constitutes the fulfilling karma (*paripūraka-karma*). This is the initial habituation to sexual misconduct.

△ Regarding "the correct arousal of ignorance": this refers to the nine underlying tendencies (anuśaya)—namely, delusion, greed, hatred, pride, and so forth—which act as the auxiliary causes for its arousal.
Because sexual conduct arises due to the afflictions of greed, delusion, and the rest, sexual desire is that which is aroused. △ Regarding "root and derivative [afflictions]":

the six root afflictions and the twenty derivative afflictions are all as previously described in the section on the habituation of greed. △ Regarding "existence and the requisites for existence": in regard to...
This refers to the arising of greed for various objects. △ Regarding "hell" (dīyù): it is a prison beneath the earth;
a "prison" (yù) implies confinement, a place where sinners are restricted and detained. In Sanskrit, *niraya* means "place of no going"; *naraka* means "vessel for suffering.
△ *Utpala* means "blue lotus," referring to a color like that of frozen, dark-blue sludge; *pundarika* means "white."
The *padma* and *pāṇḍurapadma* are both red lotuses, and their colors are like this. The eight cold hells are: 1. Arbuda (Blisters), 2.
Nirarbuda (Cracked Blisters), 3. Aṭaṭa (Shivering), 4. Hahava (Lamentation), 5. Huhuva (Moaning), 6. Utpala (Blue Lotus), 7. Padma (Red Lotus), and 8. Mahāpadma (Great Red Lotus).
The eight hot hells are: 1. Saṃjīva (Reviving), 2. Kālasūtra (Black Rope), 3. Raurava (Crying Out), and 4. [Mahāraurava]... [Text continues].
1. Great Screaming (Mahāraurava); 2. Fivefold Burning Heat (Tapana); 3. Sixfold Extreme Burning Heat (Pratāpana); 4. Universal Burning Heat (Sampratapana); 5. Uninterrupted (Avīci).

△ This refers to the miasmic vapors of the ocean. △ When humans inhale them, they immediately fall ill. △ It means to collide or clash. △ It means to encounter with hostility or to act in opposition. △ Fire can cast objects;
because of the fire of hatred (*dveṣa*), it casts forth various instruments of golden suffering. △ "Mutilation" refers to men.

Because their power was removed, it is called "castration"; because the women were confined within the palace, it is called "palace" (gōng); furthermore, "castration" refers to cutting off the ears. △ Regarding the "Five Punishments of Qin":
these were established by the Qin Chancellor Gongsun Yang (Shangjun). They are: first, the tattooing punishment (carving characters on the forehead and marking them with ink);

second, the *ní* punishment (cutting off the nose); third, the *fèi* punishment (cutting off the feet); fourth, the *gōng* punishment; and fifth, the great execution (capital punishment). These new Five Punishments are those of the Han dynasty.

The "Zheng-hou" (Punishment for the Marquis of Zheng) was that established by Xiao He. A *chai* (strip) signifies shame; a *bian* (whip) is used to turn the skin blue, symbolizing the Eastern direction and the wood element of the *bing-yi* days.
It has five grades, from ten to fifty strokes, with each increment of ten strokes requiring a redemption of one *jin* of copper.

The second type of staff, the *bian*, is used until blood appears, symbolizing the Southern direction and the fire element of the *bing-ding* days. It also has five grades, from sixty to one hundred strokes. The third is called *tu* (servitude).
This is a slave who is driven by day; in the west, under the metal of Geng and Xin, he is restrained at night.
This also consists of five grades over one year (twenty *jin*), one and a half years (thirty *jin*), two years (forty *jin*), two and a half years (fifty *jin*), and three years (sixty *jin*).
The four flows disperse like water flowing eastward, never returning west again; the black water symbolizes the north.
In the directions of Ren and Kui (North), there are three grades of water: two thousand li, two thousand five hundred li, and three thousand li.
When one dies, the flesh and bones return to the earth; the earth is yellow, symbolizing the central element of Wu and Ji (Earth). △ "Yan" also means to extend or draw forth.
△ "Jiào" (校) is the same as "jiā" (枷, a wooden collar). The *Yì* says: "Carrying the collar, his ears are destroyed. △ "A large tail and a long beard" refers to the poem which says:
"The wolf paws at its beard and treads upon its tail. △ "Sharp-headed" means its head is pointed; the *Wénxuǎn* says: "Sharp-eared and white-headed.
△ "Flying mind" means its mind is restless and active. △ "Like dust following the wind, each has no fixed place."

As for "the observer," both the wind and the minute particles are individually invisible; though the particles possess form, they are not illuminated without the sun—this is used as a metaphor for those who harbor wickedness and are not perceived by others.
△ "Like splitting" means like splitting the five fingers. △ "The carriage cage" refers to the device used to restrain and confine criminals.
△ "Accumulating evil" means harboring malice in one's heart; it is like concealing resentment while appearing to be a friend.
If one writes the character *jin* (槿), it is confused with the aforementioned *tou-le* (投礰); if one writes the character *pao* (拋), it is confused with the aforementioned *zhi* (擲).

△ *Sakāya* is translated here as "false view" (*mithyādṛṣṭi*). △ Regarding the "clinging to views and precepts": "view" refers to the two views of self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*);

"precepts" refers to the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*); and "clinging" refers to the clinging to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*). If these five are grasped as eternal, one contradicts [the truth of] annihilation; if grasped as annihilated, then...
Because it contravenes the constant [nature of reality], it is called "arising in opposition"; its manifestation issues from resistance and rejection. △ "Defiled wisdom" refers to false knowledge.
△ "Adherence to views" refers to taking one's own views regarding objects as the most excellent among all views. △ "Rituals and observances" refers to maintaining precepts based on such views;
for example, non-Buddhists, through their divine eye, observe that chickens and dogs die and are reborn in heaven, and thus claim that this alone is sufficient.
When chickens and dogs die, they are all reborn in heaven; consequently, people observe the "chicken precept" and the "dog precept.

This is like one who, when accused in a lawsuit regarding food stored overnight, conceals his own transgressions until they are exposed by the accusations of others. △ "Pursuing and provoking to violent heat" means pursuing the faults and evils of others and provoking their minds to become violently agitated.
△ "Stinging maggots" refers to complaining about another's affairs, which is like insects or venomous creatures inflicting injury upon a person.

The second section, "The Mutual Retribution of the Twelve," first provides a general summary. Regarding the six consciousnesses as the creators of karma: the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) are merely the instruments for creating karma, like nets for fish or birds;

it is the six consciousnesses that actually create it. Furthermore, there is a distinction between primary and auxiliary creation: the sixth consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is the primary creator, while the five preceding consciousnesses are the auxiliary creators.
Regarding the karma of total retribution: this refers to projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karman*). Among all types of karma, this is the most predominant.

Therefore, it is precisely because [the seventh consciousness] can induce and produce the various realms of existence (gati). Regarding wholesome and unwholesome volition (*cetanā*): this is the very essence of karma.

Wholesome volition serves as the cause for wholesome retribution, while unwholesome volition serves as the cause for unwholesome retribution. Based on the causes created by the first six consciousnesses, the eighth [consciousness] undergoes the retribution, which is neutral (*avyākṛta*).
Regarding "powerful and conforming transformation": the first five [consciousnesses] cannot create or induce [karmic results], but merely follow along with the sixth.
When the sixth consciousness is active and the performance of good is powerful, the first five consciousnesses follow suit in performing good;

when the performance of evil is powerful, the first five consciousnesses follow suit in performing evil. ▲ First, the retribution of seeing: △ Because form can enslave the mind and cause it to become agitated, a blazing fire appears.
△ "Various evil things" refers to iron mountains, iron cities, ox-headed hell-wardens, wounds, swords, blades, weapons, and so forth. ▲ Second.
[The text] reports: △ Rain, mist, and venomous insects constitute the realm of the body. △ Venomous vapors constitute the realm of the nose (and so forth).
▲ Third, the retribution of smelling. △ "Nai" (餒) refers to spoiled fish; "shuang" (爽) refers to spoiled broth—meaning they have become rotten and lost their freshness.
As Laozi said: "The five flavors cause the mouth to lose its sense of taste. △ "To practice the Way" means to tread upon the Way. △
The *guān* (觀) refers to the two watchtowers (*què*) at the entrance of a gate. According to ancient and modern legal texts, the term *què* signifies a watchtower.
In antiquity, two watchtowers were erected before each gate to mark the palace entrance. As for the term *guān*, it means that one may ascend it to observe things from afar.

When ministers were about to attend court, they would reflect upon their own deficiencies (*què*) upon reaching this place; this is why it is so called. △ The character *zì* (倳) refers to the sharp edge of bamboo. Furthermore—

"Zuò" (倳) means to thrust an object into the ground; [the character] "sī" (思) implies the desire for retribution. △ Wind is able to transform with rapidity and lacks a fixed form, resembling the swiftness of the mind.
△ "Huáng" (荒) means chaos or disorder. △ Objects such as stones and the like should be considered the objective sphere of the body.
Second, specifically clarifying the heavy and light [karmic weight]. △ Regarding the "six faculties and ten causes being fully present for simultaneous creation":
this refers to when the eye-faculty creates evil, the remaining five faculties are simultaneously present and complete in creating the ten causes. △ Regarding "not involving other faculties":

this refers to when visual consciousness and the mind (manas) create karma; it is only the eye-faculty and the eye-object that create together, without concurrently involving other faculties or objects.

△ Regarding "neither mouth nor mind acts": this means that while the body commits killing, stealing, or sexual misconduct, the mouth does not give rise to the four evils, and the mind is free from greed, hatred, and delusion.
Alternatively, it may mean that the mind creates the three evils while the body and mouth do not act upon them;

or it may mean that the body, mouth, and mind all commit killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct—meaning the mind intends it, the mouth speaks of it, and the body performs it. △ Regarding "the three karmas are not simultaneous":
Not possessing all three—killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct—means either that at the time of killing one does not simultaneously commit stealing or sexual misconduct;

or that when committing killing or stealing, one does not concurrently commit sexual misconduct; or that when committing sexual misconduct or killing, one does not commit stealing. This refers solely to cases where the offenses are not committed in their entirety.
Regarding "committing a single offense": this means that at the time one commits a single action, one neither intends it in the mind nor expresses it through speech.
Alternatively, it may be that the former two karmas constitute this single karma (and so forth).

Second, the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta-gati*). △ Regarding the lack of restraint in heavy and light [offenses]: there are ten grave offenses and forty-eight secondary ones. △ Regarding "destroying the Buddha's *nirvāṇa*":

this refers to not believing in the existence of a place of ultimate peace and bliss. △ Regarding "not being subject to light retribution": this does not mean that one has merely created objects of greed.

After these ten types of offenses, one receives only the light retribution of the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*); this implies that after having already exhausted the heavy suffering of hell, one then undergoes the retribution of a ghost.
△ The *pāpagha* ghost is the ghost of drought; some scriptures refer to it as the "yao" (妖) ghost, meaning a seductive spirit that deludes and confuses people because of its excessive passions.
△ Regarding the instruments of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*): they consist of various things that run counter to one's heart.

This is the realm [of such things]. △ Regarding the transformation of water and stones into monsters: the *Analects* (Kongzi Shijia) states, "I have heard that among the monsters of stone are the *wanglang*, and among the monsters of water are the *long* and the *wangxiang*;
some say they are the one-legged *wanglang*, the essence of the mountains. They delight in learning human speech and are able to bewilder people.
△ As for the teacher of children, this refers to the *Mingdong* (Cockcrow); both cause and effect and retribution are entirely illusory and false.

Since the creation of sensation, if examined thoroughly and constantly, is entirely unattainable, it is said: "If one awakens to the fact that Bodhi is fundamentally non-existent, then the three realms of animal existence [are likewise so].
△ "Guizheng" (咎徵) refers to the evidence or omen of evil conduct. △ The "Diao-yang" ([(嫡-女)*鳥]) is the *yin* bird; thus it presides over rain. A popular proverb says:

"When the Diao-yang dances, there will be great rain throughout the world. △ Regarding the crane (*he*), the *Xiang He Jing* (Treatise on the Characteristics of Cranes) states: "It is a bird of the Yang."
For this reason, the lordly crane can alert others to the dew; when the dew falls, it cries. △ The fox is a demonic beast; the *Shuowen* says that the fox possesses three virtues:
its color is neutral and harmonious, its forequarters are small while its hindquarters are large, and it dies with its head resting upon a mound.

The *Mountains and Rivers Record* (*Shanhai jing*) states that the fox was formerly a licentious woman of antiquity; her name was Zi, and she transformed into a fox. △ As for those that respond to the seasons, there are the swallows.

The wild goose (*hàn*) and the swallow (*yàn*) know the community; the former leaves the community while the latter arrives. The ancient and modern commentaries state that the swallow is also called *tiānnǚ* (Celestial Woman) and is also termed a "fierce bird" (*zhìniǎo*).
A poem says: "The swallows fly, their wings fluttering slowly. As for the wild goose, it is a bird that follows the sun; the *Lǐjì* states:
"In the month of the last autumn, the wild geese arrive as guests. △ The "Qilin and Feng" refers to the Qilin and the Phoenix. The male is called... [text ends]
The *Shuowen* says that the *qilin* is a "benevolent beast," while the *Shiyi* says it is a horse with yellow feet, round hooves, and fleshy tips on its horns;
its sound accords with the *huangzhong* pitch-pipe, and it appears when a king possesses supreme benevolence. The phoenix is a divine bird:
the male is called the *feng* and the female the *huang*. It is a creature of the *chunhu* mansion and the essence of Yang. The *Ruyingtu* states that when a king... [appears].
This is an auspicious omen; when encountering chaos, one dwells among the barbarians.

The destinies of these four types of people can be clearly seen. ▲ The destiny of the five immortals. △ Those who cause the lowly to become noble, such as those who point at objects and turn them into gold.
△ The "honor and defense" (rōei) are the two qi of yin and yang within the body. △ "The source of all transformation" refers to knowing the One.
The transformation of all things is the source [of this]. These ten kinds of immortals do not leave the human realm;
rather, they dwell in transformed gardens, pavilions, manors, and residences at famous peaks and numinous mountains, such as Fangzhang and Penglai.
For example, in the fifth year of the Yongping era of Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty, Liu Nong of Shan County entered Mount Tiantai; while crossing the mountain, he saw a great stream.
The two women were of such exquisite beauty that he remained with them for half a year. Later, out of homesickness, they requested to return.
Once they had left, he found that his relatives and old acquaintances had vanished, the towns and houses had changed beyond recognition, and there was no one he knew.
Upon inquiring in detail, he learned that their family was now in its seventh generation of descendants; thus he knew they were all of the class of immortals.

The Celestial Realm of Desire. △ Regarding "Celestial" (*deva*): it is the natural fruit of retribution; because they do not rely on human effort or thought to obtain clothing—clothing comes to them—and food—food arrives of its own accord—they are called "Celestials.
In secular exegesis, it is said that "Celestial" means "manifest"; they are manifest as they occupy a high and prominent position.

Furthermore, "Celestial" means "level and open"; they are level, open, lofty, and remote. In spring, it is called the "Azure Heaven" (*cāngtiān*), for the Yang energy begins to emerge and its color is azure.
In summer it is called the Azure Heaven (*cāṅ yě*), for its qi is spread out and vast. In autumn it is called the Compassionate Heaven (*míntiān*);
"mín" means pity, for when things wither and fall, they are pitiable and tragic. In winter it is called the Upper Heaven (*shàngtiān*), for its qi ascends and is severed from the earth.
Thus, the lifespan of these six heavens is as explained in the *Abhidharmakośa*: fifty human years constitute one day and night for the first heaven.
At night, one shall receive this longevity, increasing fivefold for each of the five hundred [years], and so forth. First, regarding the Four Heavenly Kings:
among those whose minds do not stray toward sexual misconduct, this is merely one example cited;

one must fully observe the five precepts—namely, refraining from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, and drinking intoxicants—and concurrently practice the ten superior wholesome deeds (*daśa-kuśala-karma-patha*) to be reborn there.

Those who desire to be born naturally in this realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*) are born among the six heavens of the desire realm; those who additionally possess a mind that protects the Dharma are born among the four heavens;

those who additionally possess a mind of compassionate transformation are born in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. Those whose minds are subtle, wondrous, skillful, and fully matured are born in the Yāma Heaven; those who additionally cultivate meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) and gather both coarse and subtle mindfulness are born in the Tuṣita Heaven;
those who cultivate the desire-realm concentration are born in the Nirmāṇarati Heaven; and those who cultivate the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*) are born in the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven.

By overcoming the obstacles of conditioned phenomena, one is born in the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations (*Paranirmita-vaśavartin*). Forty thousand *yojanas* from the human realm, halfway up Mount Sumeru, there are four terraces.

On these dwell the Four Great Kings—Dhṛtarāṣṭra in the east, Virūḍhaka in the south, Virūpākṣa in the west, and Vaiśravaṇa in the north—who together lead the eight classes of spirits and deities. Above them, the Trāyastriṃśa gods reside upon the summit of Mount Sumeru.
The *Śāstra* says: At the summit of Mount Sumeru, the Eighty-thousand [yojana-high] Heaven of the Thirty-three (*Trāyastriṃśa*) resides.
At its four corners there are four peaks, inhabited by the Vajra-headed ones; the central palace is named Sudarśana, measuring ten thousand *yojanas* in circumference.

These four peaks are the abodes of the thirty-two heavens. △ "Li" (戾) means to oppose or to deviate; it refers to being unable to oppose or deviate from their intent. △ Regarding the three calamities (*saṃvartanī*): [text fragment].
The word "and" (*ca*) refers here to the abode of Maitreya; other ordinary devas still undergo destruction by the three calamities.

△ Regarding the "vessel-world" (*bhājana-loka*), this refers to the environmental support (*āśraya-pratyaya*). △ Regarding the "six who experience desire," this means that the two classes of earth-dwelling devas engage in physical union like humans;
in the Yāma heaven they embrace; in the Tuṣita heaven they hold hands; in the Nirmāṇarati heaven they smile at one another; and in the Paranirmita-vaśavartin heaven [they gaze at each other].
Mutual gazing is collectively termed "desire. The *Loutan jing* (Lokānuvartana-sūtra) states: In the [Heaven of] the Earth-Dwellers (*bhūmi-cara*), there is physical union without emission;

in the Yama Heaven, they embrace; in the Tuṣita Heaven, they merely hold hands; in the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, they rejoice through speech and laughter; in the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, they merely gaze at one another;

and in the [Heaven of] Others' Creations, they do so by merely hearing sounds and smelling fragrances. The robes of these six heavens all weigh half a *liang*; according to the *Āgama*, those of the [first] four heavens weigh half of that.
In the Trāyastriṃśa heaven it is six *liang*; in Yama, three *liang*; in Tuṣita, one and a half *liang*; in Nirmāṇarati, one *liang*; and in Paranirmitavaśavartin, half a *liang*.

△ Although the forms differ and their movements are not the same as those of humans, because the characteristics of desire in the human realm are coarse and defiled, they are here described as "emerging and moving.
(The following enters the Ninth Scripture.)

Second, the heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) that precede those of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) also consist of form-dharmas (*rūpa-dharma*). Because their three types of desire and five kinds of exquisite objects are superior, they are designated merely by the name "desire.

This [designation] is based on the excellence of their form-dharmas. Furthermore, all their environments and personal adornments are produced from meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), being distinct from the distracted movements of the lower realms;
therefore, they receive the title of "meditation" (*dhyāna*). The celestial garments of these gods are no different from those of the desire-realm gods.
Although they lack topknots, they resemble celestial crowns; they have no distinction between male and female forms, and their appearance is of a single kind.

In the Sanskrit language, *dhyāna* is translated here as "quiet contemplation" (*jinglü*), which is a term for the equalization of concentration and wisdom. It is also called the "Forest of Merit," among other names.

In this heaven, there is no difference between day and night, and their lifespan and physical stature are equal in number. [Excluding those in the Heaven of Non-conception, these are included within the extensive classification.]
This refers to the *phala-devas*. △ Regarding the Mahāsāṃghika school: within the Vinaya, there are the Sthavira and Mahāsāṃghika schools. △ Regarding the "six practices":
one cultivates the contemplation of the six matters to subdue the afflictions; this is also called the "twelve-fold contemplation," as cause and effect are combined.

The first [stage] is taken as the cause and reaching the earth as the fruit; the initial aversion is the cause and departing from the lower realms is the fruit—this refers to the aversion toward the desires of the lower realms.

The realm [of form] is suffering, coarse, and an obstruction; to long for the realm of form is to seek what is pure, sublime, and free. △ Those who generate [attachment] by savoring this possess outflow-tainted minds;

as they cultivate the various branches [of concentration], they frequently give rise to attachment, which immediately leads to the ripening of results and rebirth, such that they do not escape the three realms.
△ As for "dwelling alone," the Heavenly King first dwells there for one kalpa, and thereafter...

The heterodox view arises: he conceives of his kinsmen and the sons of Brahmā as suddenly coming into being. △ Regarding "without vitarka and with only vicāra": because coarse thought (*vitarka*) has been severed, there is no *vitarka*;

because subtle perception (*vicāra*) remains, there is *vicāra*. △ Regarding "the master of the single cause": they reckon that the self (*ātman*) is the cause capable of producing the host of Brahmās. △ Regarding the "eight sufferings":
birth, old age, sickness, death, separation from the beloved, meeting with the hated, not obtaining what one seeks... [and so forth].

This refers to attaining the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*). △ Regarding "not manifesting body or mind within the three realms": if one stills the body and withdraws the thoughts to enter meditative absorption (*samādhi*), that is the manifestation of body and mind.
