△ "Even if there is the principle of arising" refers to the existence of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).

Although this aggregate of formations exists, because it is equivalent to grass and trees, one knows that it too returns to non-existence. Since it cannot be apprehended in the present, one should know that after death, the four aggregates likewise [cease].

Furthermore, when emptiness is discussed in conjunction with cause and effect, it is termed the "Eight Signless" (*aṣṭānimitta*). Among these eight: △ Regarding the inclusion of the cessation of sensation and perception (*vedanā-saṃjñā-nirodha*):

this is a brief mention based on the fact that the two aggregates [of sensation and perception] have already ceased. By taking the example that the existing formations (*saṃskāra*) are not non-existent, one knows that the three aggregates which have already ceased are likewise not non-existent.

By taking the example that the three aggregates which have already ceased are now not existent, one knows that the currently existing aggregate of formations is likewise not existent. Therefore, by means of existence and cessation...

By analogy, four propositions are established: neither existence nor non-existence. Since the four aggregates (*skandhas*) of the present life are neither existent nor non-existent, the four aggregates after death are likewise neither existent nor non-existent;
therefore, they are called the "eightfold negation" (*aṣṭavidha-ubhaya-niṣedha*). Regarding the refutation of the essential nature (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa-bhaṅga*), each proposition is self-sublated:
the conceptualization of existence is negated by its very being non-existent, and the conceptualization of non-existence is negated by its very being existent.
Thus, it constitutes a contradiction of its own characteristics. △ Regarding "attaining any one condition":

if, within one aggregate (skandha), one perceives that after death there is neither existence nor non-existence, one knows that the same applies to the other aggregates. ▲ Among the nine [sections], △ the seven limits refer to the seven places of retribution:
1. humans; 2. devas; 3. the first dhyāna; 4. the second dhyāna; 5. the third dhyāna; 6. the fourth dhyāna.
The seven formless realms: when the retribution of these seven stations is exhausted, they all return to cessation and extinction, never to continue again.
Among the ten [realms], five locations are currently *nirvāṇa* itself; there is no other place of peace and bliss apart from them.

Because one practices the concentration of desire and perceives the mark of perfect clarity, one then reckons the desire realm to be *nirvāṇa*. Because the first dhyāna is free from sorrow, one then claims—
Nirvāṇa, etc. △ "The supreme pure basis" (*viśuddha-āśraya*) is another name for Nirvāṇa.
The five aggregates of consciousness (*pañca-vijñāna-skandha*). △ "The deep, subtle cords and knots": this is a simultaneous presentation of both the dharma and its metaphor;

the deep and subtle *saṃskāra-skandha* (aggregate of formations) acts as the causal agent that brings about [rebirth]. △ The *pudgala* (person) is the fruit brought about by that cause. △ "Deep channels": the *saṃskāra-skandha* is subtle like these.

The blood vessels within the body are profound and subtle, difficult to discern. △ Regarding "essence-color" (*jingse*): "essence" refers to the clarity and brilliance, while "color" refers to its manifestation;

furthermore, because it is the essence of the Great Yang, it is called "essence-color. △ Regarding "innermost": the former refers to the contemplation of internal illumination, while the latter refers to the internal realm that is illuminated.

Since the consciousness-aggregate (*vijñānaskandha*) has reached its ultimate limit, there are no further delusive phenomena beyond this to be illuminated; hence it is said, "there is nothing [further]."

Because there is no karma that leads one into the various realms of existence upon entry, it is said that "no class of beings can summon [them]. Regarding "sight and hearing pervade and connect with the neighboring":
this means that seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are harmoniously integrated and interfused as a single entity.

"First, the grasping at causes and their origins. "Those for whom birth-and-death has already ceased" refers to those who have already extinguished the arising and ceasing of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations), yet because the subtle consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) still remains, it is said that "its essence is refined but not yet perfected.

"Awareness and cognition are interpenetrating" means that seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are fused and integrated into one. "It is entirely the shadow of consciousness" means that it arises as a transformation of True Suchness (*tathatā*).

It is also an image. △ Regarding "the cause and that which is caused": by means of the cause and the object of causation, deluded consciousness clings to it as being truly eternal, serving as the cause that gives rise to the myriad dharmas; this is precisely clinging to the false as true.

△ Regarding "that to which one returns," the *pradhāna* (primordial matter) is simply consciousness itself, yet it is falsely reckoned as the ultimate nirvana to which one returns. △ Regarding "that which is attained within the cause," it is reckoned...

There exists this reality from which one may attain the fruit and the state of ultimate peace and happiness to which one returns. Regarding the second [section], concerning "the capable and the incapable":
it is not merely cognition that serves as the cause; rather, it is said to belong to the essence of the self (*ātman*).

As for what is propounded by the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), the non-Buddhists reckon that the sixth [consciousness] of the desire realm is eternal and capable of generating all derivative states; they hold that their own mind acts as the causal agent for these various phenomena.

"Arising" refers to the fruit of an activity; because it is accomplished by means of that activity, it is called "activity. Among the three [aggregates], regarding the arising and ceasing within the aggregate of birth:
those who prematurely calculate [the mind] as permanent are those who, amidst the arising and ceasing of consciousness, falsely reckon it to be permanent.

Furthermore, they see the immobility of consciousness amidst the arising and ceasing of the aggregate of formations and prematurely calculate it to be permanent. Alternatively, the character "zǎo" (prematurely) should perhaps be read as "wàng" (falsely).
The character "筆" (pen) is an error. Regarding the fourth [point]: "Accomplishing false and erroneous fruits" refers to the deluded calculation that after death one becomes grass or trees;
since this principle does not exist in reality, it is called "false and erroneous. Regarding the fifth [point]:

"Observing the accomplishment of dust" means observing that the characteristics of the earth-element (*pṛthivī-mahābhūta*) are quiescent and unmoving; furthermore, it means that accumulated dust can form a world. "All things, too... [is as follows].

Thus, by means of the faculties, one attains their mutual interchangeability; consequently, one calculates that upon every single object, a superior function can be activated to achieve a superior fruit.
Since objects possess cognition, they too can be cultivated to perfection, and thus cognition and vision may together attain permanence;

for this reason, one venerates fire and other elements. Among the six types of [false] reckonings, the reckoning of "clarity within emptiness" refers to the movement of arising and ceasing when the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) has already ceased.

They erroneously reckon this consciousness-aggregate (*vijñāna-skandha*) as being perfectly luminous, empty, and still. △ "Not extinguishing the manifold transformations" means that one has already eliminated the preceding four aggregates;

thus it is said "extinguish the manifold transformations. Furthermore, because one has already shattered the basis for the production of transformations within the category of the activity-aggregate (*saṃskāra-skandha*), it is called "the manifold transformations.
▲ In the seventh [section], △ "Láo" (labor/exhaustion) and "Láo" (firm/strong) were used interchangeably in antiquity. ▲ In the eighth [section], △ "Mutually" (hù).
As for "mutual penetration," consciousness serves as the life-root; since both self and others take this consciousness as their life, they penetrate one another.
△ Fearing that [the life-force] would be exhausted: if one does not crave desire, consciousness will not continue; if consciousness does not continue, the life-force is exhausted;
therefore, one retains the dusts of worldly toil. △ Regarding the "Woman-Jewel" (*nārī-ratna*): the *Erya* states, "The male jewel is called a *yan*; the female jewel is called a *yuan*."
In the section on the exhortation to practice: △ "Because of relying on delusion" means that delusion arises because one does not understand consciousness.

△ "One who has previously practiced a deluded mind" refers to having habitually perfumed this nature of inverted delusion within the consciousness in past lives; it is now triggered and manifested by meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Since this is entirely cessation (*śamatha*) accompanied by contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), it is called "vipaśyanā within śamatha. △ "The defilements of the mind are washed away" means...
Because the mind is not defiled by the taints of Māra, it is said to be "washed away. △ Regarding "stripping off" (tì): the *Yí* says, "In the context of litigation, one receives garments;
he is given a *pán* (a large sash). He strips off this sash three times during the morning. △ Regarding "inferior ones who advance":
the practice of the two vehicles is inferior, yet because they have distanced themselves from Māra, they are able to progress toward the Great Practice.
Second, within the section "Distinct Manifestation through Ānanda’s Hearing and Requesting Instruction," it says: "Certainly not of the same category as deluded thought.
The meaning is that because its substance is of the same category as deluded thought, it is able to accommodate the perception of water and the perception of sourness;

thus, one knows that it is not only the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) that is deluded thought. "Because it arises from sensation (*vedanā*), it can move the substance of form" reveals that sensation, too, is [deluded thought].
If it were not for conceptualization (*vikalpa*), how could the reception of sensations cause the physical substance of form to undergo increase or decrease?
△ As for the dissolution of the material body, it occurs through the power of mental conception;

thus one may transform the body, as in the cases of the "Widow’s Rock" or the "Aunt’s Spring," or as the youth Candraprabha transformed his body into water through thought. Because such powers can sit and contemplate the world beneath heaven, it is so called.
It is called "transforming images" because the penetrating mind can transform all images and take them as objects.

△ It is said that "seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are not excluded" because the substance of consciousness is hidden and secret; thus, it is represented by means of its functional manifestations.

△ It is said that "it does not tolerate habitual delusions" because if this were truly real, it would be inconsistent for it to allow habitual delusions to manifest within it. △ "The measure of habituation" refers to this: [End of segment]
This refers to the subtle traces of habitual tendencies within seeing and hearing. △ "Entangled form" (*wangxiang*) means being formless. △ Regarding "the profound entry merges with the profound":

the upper "profound" refers to the contemplation that subdues the arising and ceasing of the *skandha* of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*); the lower "profound" refers to merging back into the clarity and stillness of the *skandha* of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).
Alternatively, it may mean that the concentration of clarified stillness merges back into the principle of profound quiescence; this "principle" is the ultimate limit of consciousness.
Furthermore: "The sun rises and the infant is born" means that when the sun rises, it appears all at once in its full roundness;

when the infant is born, the six sense faculties are simultaneously complete—this is a metaphor for sudden enlightenment regarding principle (*li*). That the sun gradually ascends and the infant gradually grows up—this is a metaphor for the gradual fulfillment of phenomena (*shi*).
Third, the circulation [of the teaching]. △ Regarding the seven treasures, there are three types: first, the seven treasures of the ocean, namely:
white silver, gold, coral, white pearls, tridacna shell, moon-pearls, and maṇi jewels; second, the seven treasures of the human world, namely:
gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, pearls, tridacna shell, and agate; third, the seven treasures of the universal wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin), which are vast and so forth.
Maitreya’s verse also says: "Vast, foremost, and eternal; its mind is not inverted. Currently, it only lacks the phrase "a mind that is not inverted.
If one wishes to include it, it is simply that practicing generosity without seeking fame and so forth constitutes a non-inverted mind.

Regarding the seven treasures of a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*): the wheel-treasure, the white elephant, the dark-blue horse, the divine jewel, the jade woman, the householder-treasure, and the military commander-treasure. These abide [in their respective realms].
During the kalpa when the human lifespan is eighty thousand years, it is precisely at that time that a Wheel-Turning King transforms the world.
△ A mere blink of an eye passes from this direction to another; because karma is so fierce and intense, one falls into hell like an arrow shot.

△ "Manifestly lacking the function of a monk" means one is incapable of performing ritual acts together with the Great Sangha; it is also translated as "extremely evil," because upon death one falls into an extremely evil place. △
The ten grave offenses are: killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, drinking intoxicants, praising oneself, disparaging others, and speaking of the faults of lay or ordained bodhisattvas;
as well as covetousness, malice, and slandering the Triple Gem. △ A single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*) is the most minimal fraction of mind and the most subtle particle of form.
A "fraction of a kṣaṇa" (śāva-kṣaṇa) is the most minute division of time. Regarding "the cause of suffering becoming a land of peace and bliss":
it means transforming the three paths into the three virtues; one is able to eliminate extreme suffering and instead experience supreme bliss. Regarding "the purity of the person who speaks":
this is not speaking with a mind of gain, fame, or arising-and-ceasing thoughts. Regarding "the purity of the Dharma spoken": it is the teaching of the true nature of reality (dharmatā).
This is the ultimate Dharma. △ Regarding "purity of the fruit," it means not allowing one to attain the fruits of humans, devas, or the two vehicles.

Third, the summary of dedication is the section on the circulation of the commentary; that is, dedicating the merit of composing this commentary to universally benefit oneself and others, so that all may together reach the secret treasury.
△ As for "dedication," it refers to what is called turning phenomena toward principle, and turning causes toward...

Regarding the turning [of the mind] toward the fruit, from self toward others, and from phenomena toward principle: fundamentally, it is because principle is inherently complete that phenomenal functions arise;
all cultivation and realization do not transcend the nature of principle. Now, one turns this mind toward the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). As for turning from self toward others:

if one is deluded regarding the pervasiveness of principle, whatever wholesome deeds one cultivates merely adorn one's own person; now, knowing that the essence of self and others is equal, one accords with [this truth].
Because of the fundamental nature, one dedicates [merit] to sentient beings. Regarding the dedication from cause to fruit: the seeds of goodness cultivated do not tend toward the Two Vehicles;

rather, what is cultivated accords with the fundamental nature and all becomes the "cause of fulfillment" (*pariniṣpanna-hetu*). Since a cause must necessarily manifest its fruit, one dedicates it to Bodhi.
Only through such dedication is there the great practice of a Bodhisattva, and only then does one achieve the equal liberation of both self and others.
